name: Manufacturing Science
source: agent-written from the MANIT 2025-26 syllabus, the course book 'Introduction to Manufacturing Processes and Workshop Technology', the usual workshop-technology texts (Hajra Choudhury, Raghuwanshi) and the conventions of first-year workshop manuals; importance is an ESTIMATE until past papers are imported
exam_notes: Theory is mini test 10, mid term 20 (1 hour) and end term 40 (2 hours). Questions are short and descriptive: name and sketch a tool, list its uses, differentiate two things, write steps; the reliable numericals are vernier/micrometer readings, pattern dimensions from allowances and the odd duty-cycle or tap-drill sum. The practical (records and viva 30, mid 20, end 40) is a job made in the shop plus a viva on the same tools, so the workshop manual has to be read properly, not skimmed.

topics.why: Usually a 2-3 mark definition or classification question and a viva opener; it also explains why the job is mild steel and the file is high carbon steel.
topics.gist:
Engineering metals are split first into **ferrous** (iron is the main constituent) and **non-ferrous** (everything else).

**Ferrous metals** are graded by carbon content. *Wrought iron* is almost pure iron (below about 0.1% C) with slag fibres; it is soft, ductile and forgeable. *Steel* carries up to about 1.5% C (some books say 2%): **mild / low carbon steel** (about 0.05-0.3% C) is what the fitting and welding jobs are made of because it is cheap, soft enough to file and saw, and weldable; **medium carbon** (0.3-0.6%) goes into shafts, axles and rails; **high carbon** (0.6-1.5%) into files, chisels, punches, springs and hacksaw blades, which are hardened so that they cut mild steel. *Cast iron* (about 2-4.5% C) is brittle but casts well, damps vibration and is strong in compression, hence machine beds, surface plates and vice bodies. *Alloy steels* add Cr, Ni, W, V: stainless steel (at least about 10.5% Cr), high speed steel (18-4-1 W-Cr-V) for drills and taps.

**Non-ferrous metals**: aluminium (light, 2.7 g/cc, good conductor), copper (electrical wiring), zinc, lead, tin, nickel, and their alloys: **brass** (Cu + Zn), **bronze** (Cu + Sn), **gunmetal** (Cu + Sn + Zn), solder (Sn + Pb), duralumin (Al + Cu + Mg + Mn). Non-ferrous metals generally do not rust, are non-magnetic and are costlier.

Know the property words too: ductility, malleability, hardness, toughness, brittleness, elasticity, plasticity, castability, weldability, machinability.
key_points: Ferrous = iron-based; non-ferrous = not iron-based (Al, Cu, Zn, Pb, Sn, Ni and their alloys)
Carbon ranges: wrought iron below ~0.1%, steel up to ~1.5% (some texts 2%), cast iron ~2-4.5%
Mild steel 0.05-0.3% C: workshop jobs, structural sections; medium 0.3-0.6%: shafts, rails; high 0.6-1.5%: files, chisels, springs
Cast iron: brittle, good castability, vibration damping, strong in compression; used for machine beds, surface plates, vice bodies
Brass = Cu + Zn; bronze = Cu + Sn; gunmetal = Cu + Sn + Zn (about 88-10-2); solder = Sn + Pb
HSS (18% W, 4% Cr, 1% V) for drills and taps; stainless steel has at least ~10.5% Cr
Ductility = drawn into wire (tension); malleability = beaten into sheet (compression)
Non-ferrous: mostly corrosion resistant, non-magnetic, good conductors, costlier
traps: Brass and bronze swapped: brass has zinc, bronze has tin
Ductility and malleability used as synonyms; ductility is under tension (wire), malleability under compression (sheet)
Writing that cast iron is tough: it is hard and brittle; toughness belongs to mild steel
Calling the file mild steel; tools are hardened high carbon steel (or HSS), the job is mild steel

questions.a: Brass is copper + zinc (typically 60-70% Cu). Copper + tin is bronze.

questions.q: The carbon content of mild steel is approximately
questions.a: Mild (low carbon) steel has about 0.05-0.3% C. 0.6-1.5% is high carbon steel; 2-4.5% is cast iron.

questions.q: Files, chisels and hacksaw blades are generally made of
questions.a: Cutting tools must be harder than the mild steel job, so they are made of high carbon steel (0.6-1.5% C), hardened and tempered.

questions.q: Differentiate between ferrous and non-ferrous metals.
questions.a:
| Ferrous | Non-ferrous |
|---|---|
| Iron is the main constituent | Iron absent or minor |
| Mostly magnetic | Mostly non-magnetic |
| Rust easily | Good corrosion resistance |
| Cheaper, stronger, heavier | Costlier, lighter (Al), better conductors (Cu, Al) |
| e.g. cast iron, wrought iron, steels | e.g. Al, Cu, Zn, Pb, brass, bronze |

questions.q: Classify engineering metals with one application of each class.
questions.a:
**Ferrous:**
- Wrought iron (<0.1% C): chains, hooks, ornamental work
- Mild steel (0.05-0.3% C): structural sections, nuts, bolts, workshop jobs
- Medium carbon steel (0.3-0.6% C): shafts, axles, rails
- High carbon steel (0.6-1.5% C): files, chisels, springs
- Cast iron (2-4.5% C): machine beds, surface plates, pipes
- Alloy steels: stainless steel (cutlery), HSS (drills, taps)

**Non-ferrous:**
- Aluminium: aircraft, utensils, cables
- Copper: electrical wires
- Zinc: galvanising
- Lead: batteries
- Alloys: brass (Cu-Zn) for fittings, bronze (Cu-Sn) for bushes and bearings, gunmetal (Cu-Sn-Zn) for valves, solder (Sn-Pb) for joining

questions.q: Define ductility, malleability, toughness and brittleness.
questions.a:
- **Ductility**: the ability to be drawn into wire under tension without breaking (copper, mild steel).
- **Malleability**: the ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheet under compression (gold, aluminium, lead).
- **Toughness**: the ability to absorb energy and deform plastically before fracture, i.e. resist impact (mild steel).
- **Brittleness**: breaking with little or no plastic deformation (cast iron, glass); the opposite of ductility.

questions.q: Why is cast iron used for machine beds and surface plates even though it is brittle?
questions.a: Cast iron casts easily into complex shapes, is cheap, has high compressive strength, is dimensionally stable once stress-relieved, and its graphite flakes give excellent vibration damping and a self-lubricating, easily scraped surface. Beds and plates carry compressive and static loads, not impact, so brittleness does not matter there.

topics.why: Sketch-and-use questions (bench vice, V-block) turn up in mini tests and almost always in the viva because the student uses them every session.
topics.gist:
A fitter cannot file, saw or chip a job that moves, so the first tools are **holding / clamping tools**.

The **bench vice** (parallel-jaw vice) is the main one: a cast iron (or cast steel) body bolted to the bench, a fixed jaw, a movable jaw driven by a square-threaded screw turned by a handle, and **hardened, serrated jaw plates** that grip the work. Its size is the **width of the jaws** (typically 75-150 mm). The jaw top should be at about elbow height. For a finished surface you put **soft jaws / vice clamps** (aluminium, copper or lead caps) over the serrations so the job is not marked. Hold the job low in the jaws when filing and sawing, so it does not chatter.

Other vices: **hand vice** (small work, drilling thin pieces), **pin vice** (small diameter wire and pins), **pipe vice** (pipes, grips at four points), **leg vice** (heavy hammering, as in a smithy), **machine vice** (on the drilling machine table), **toolmaker's clamp** and **C-clamp / G-clamp**.

The **V-block** is a hardened steel or cast iron block with a 90° V groove (often grooves on two faces and a slot for a U-clamp). It holds **cylindrical work** for marking centre lines, locating centres and drilling across a shaft. V-blocks are made and used in **matched pairs** so a long shaft lies parallel to the surface plate.
key_points: Bench vice parts: body, fixed jaw, movable jaw, hardened serrated jaw plates, square-threaded screw, handle, nut, base
Vice size = width of jaws (e.g. 100 mm); a square thread is used because it transmits force with low friction loss
Soft jaws (Al, Cu, Pb) protect finished surfaces from the serrations
Job held low and close to the jaws to avoid vibration; never hammer the vice handle to tighten
Hand vice, pin vice, pipe vice, leg vice, machine vice: one use each
V-block: 90° V groove, used in pairs with a U-clamp, for marking and drilling round bars
C-clamp/G-clamp and toolmaker's clamp hold work to angle plates or two pieces together
traps: Stating vice size as its length or opening; it is the jaw width
Calling the V angle 60°; the standard V-block groove is 90°
Forgetting the soft jaws when a question asks how to hold a finished job
Leg vice is for heavy hammering, not for fine fitting

questions.q: The size of a bench vice is specified by
questions.a: A bench vice is specified by the width of its jaws, e.g. a 100 mm vice.

questions.q: The included angle of the groove of a standard V-block is
questions.a: The standard V-block has a 90° V groove so a round bar seats on two lines symmetric about the vertical.

questions.q: Which vice is best suited to holding a pipe for cutting and threading?
questions.a: The pipe vice grips the pipe at four points with serrated V jaws, so it neither slips nor gets crushed.

questions.q: Draw a neat sketch of a bench vice and name its parts.
questions.a:
**Sketch description:** a cast iron body bolted to the bench; on the left the fixed jaw cast with the body; the movable jaw slides in a rectangular guide in the body; a square-threaded screw passes through the movable jaw into a nut fixed in the body and is turned by a tommy-bar handle at the front; hardened, serrated steel jaw plates are screwed to the faces of both jaws.

**Parts:** body/base, fixed jaw, movable jaw, jaw plates (hardened, serrated), square-threaded spindle, nut, handle, guide/slide.

**Specification:** width of jaws, e.g. 100 mm. **Use:** holding work for filing, sawing, chipping, tapping.

questions.q: What is a V-block? Explain its use with a sketch description.
questions.a: A V-block is a rectangular block of hardened steel or cast iron with an accurately machined 90° V groove (usually on top and bottom, with smaller grooves on the sides) and a slot for a U-clamp. A round bar laid in the V is located with its axis parallel to the base. Uses: (i) holding cylindrical work on a surface plate for marking centre lines and centres with a surface gauge or height gauge; (ii) holding a round bar under the drill to drill a hole across the shaft. They are made in matched pairs so long shafts can be supported at both ends.

questions.q: Why are soft jaws used in a vice? Name two materials for them.
questions.a: The jaw plates are hardened and serrated and would mark or dent a finished or soft job. Soft jaws (vice clamps) are caps of a softer material placed over the jaws to grip without marking. Materials: aluminium, copper, lead, brass (also fibre or wood).

questions.q: Why is the screw of a bench vice square-threaded?
questions.a: A square thread has zero thread angle, so almost all the applied torque becomes axial clamping force (higher efficiency, less friction and less radial bursting force on the nut than a V thread). It is also strong and wears well under repeated clamping.

topics.why: Every fitting job starts with marking, so 'name, sketch and give the use of' questions on the surface plate, try square, scriber, surface gauge and combination set are standard.
topics.gist:
Marking transfers the drawing onto the metal so that sawing and filing have a line to work to. Measuring checks the result.

**Reference surfaces:** the **surface plate** (cast iron, ribbed underneath, top scraped flat; also granite) and the **marking table** give a true flat datum; the **angle plate** gives a true 90° face to clamp work against.

**Marking media:** chalk or whitewash on rough surfaces, **Prussian blue** or layout dye on finished ones, copper sulphate solution on bright mild steel (it leaves a thin copper film that shows scribed lines clearly).

**Marking tools:** the **scriber** (hardened steel point, about 12-15° included) scratches lines; the **surface gauge / scribing block** (base, spindle, adjustable scriber) scribes lines parallel to the surface plate; **dividers** and **odd-leg calipers** (see the next topic); **punches** make the lines permanent.

**Measuring and checking:** the **steel rule** (least count 0.5 mm, sometimes 1 mm), the **try square** (stock and hardened blade at 90°; checks squareness and flatness and is used for marking lines at right angles to an edge), the **combination set** (rule with square head for 90° and 45°, protractor head for any angle, centre head for finding the centre of a round bar), bevel protractor, feeler gauge, and the vernier and micrometer for precise work.
key_points: Surface plate: cast iron or granite, datum for marking; keep covered and never hammer on it
Marking media: chalk (rough), Prussian blue (finished), copper sulphate (bright mild steel)
Scriber: hardened high carbon steel, sharp point, held inclined so it trails along the straight edge
Surface gauge: base, pillar/spindle, scriber; scribes lines parallel to the datum at a set height
Try square: stock + blade at 90°; checks squareness, marks perpendicular lines; size = blade length
Combination set: steel rule + square head (90°/45°, spirit level) + protractor head + centre head
Steel rule least count 0.5 mm; measure from a graduation, not the worn end, when accuracy matters
Angle plate: two faces at 90°, slots for clamping work during marking
traps: Saying the try square measures length; it checks 90° and flatness
Mixing up the surface gauge (marking parallel lines) with the height gauge (measures height with a vernier)
Forgetting that the centre head of a combination set is what finds the centre of a round bar
Not saying which marking medium suits which surface

questions.a: The try square checks right angles and flatness and is used to mark lines perpendicular to a finished edge.

questions.q: Which part of the combination set is used to locate the centre of a round bar?
questions.a: The centre head has two arms at 90° whose bisector is the rule edge; two lines drawn at different positions on the end face intersect at the centre.

questions.q: The marking medium preferred on a bright, finished mild steel surface is
questions.a: Copper sulphate deposits a thin copper film on bright steel, and scribed lines show as bright steel lines on a copper background. (Prussian blue/layout dye also works.)

questions.q: Name any five marking tools used in the fitting shop and state the use of each.
questions.a:
1. **Surface plate**: flat datum surface for marking and checking.
2. **Scriber**: scratches (scribes) lines on metal.
3. **Surface gauge / scribing block**: scribes lines parallel to the surface plate at a set height; also checks parallelism.
4. **Try square**: marks lines at 90° to an edge, checks squareness.
5. **Dividers**: scribe circles and arcs, step off equal distances.
6. **Odd-leg calipers**: scribe lines parallel to an edge, locate the centre of a bar.
7. **Centre/prick punch**: make marked lines and centres permanent.
(Any five.)

questions.q: Describe a surface gauge with a sketch description.
questions.a: A surface gauge (scribing block) has a heavy flat cast iron base (often with a V groove underneath so it can also sit on a round bar), a vertical spindle/pillar that can be tilted, and a scriber clamped to the spindle by a snug and clamping nut, with a fine-adjustment screw. Set the scriber to the required height from a steel rule held in a rule stand, then slide the base on the surface plate so the scriber marks a line on the job parallel to the plate. It is also used to check the parallelism of surfaces and to centre work on a machine.

questions.q: What is a surface plate? Why is it made of cast iron, and how is it cared for?
questions.a: A surface plate is a rigid plate with an accurately flat (scraped or lapped) top surface used as a datum for marking out and checking flatness. Cast iron is used because it can be cast with stiffening ribs, is stable after stress relieving, resists wear, damps vibration and can be scraped flat; granite plates are also used. Care: never hammer or file on it, keep it clean and lightly oiled, cover it when not in use, and put work on it gently.

topics.topic: Files, chisels, hacksaw, punches and hammers
topics.why: The single most-asked fitting topic: file classification by cut, grade and shape, the parts of a file and hammer, hacksaw blade pitch and the punch angles appear in almost every paper and every viva.
topics.gist:
**Files** remove small amounts of metal. Parts: tang, heel, face, edge, point (tip); **length is measured from heel to point, without the tang** (100-400 mm). Files are classified by:
- **Cut**: single cut (one set of parallel teeth, about 60-65° to the axis; soft metals, sharpening), double cut (overcut plus upcut crossing, for faster removal on steel), rasp cut (separate pointed teeth, for wood, leather), curved cut (soft metals, aluminium).
- **Grade (coarseness)**: rough, bastard, second cut, smooth, dead smooth, in order of finer teeth.
- **Shape (section)**: flat, hand (one **safe edge** without teeth), square, round (rat-tail), half round, triangular, knife edge, needle files.

**Hacksaw**: frame (fixed or adjustable), blade of HSS or high carbon steel, 250 or 300 mm long between pin holes. **Teeth point away from the handle; the cut is on the forward stroke.** Pitch: about 14 teeth per 25 mm for soft and thick sections, 18 for general work, 24 for tubes and angles, 32 for thin sheet; keep at least 2-3 teeth in the section. The **set** of the teeth makes the kerf wider than the blade so it does not jam.

**Chisels**: flat, cross-cut (cape), half-round and diamond-point; the point angle is larger for harder metals (about 60° for mild steel). **Punches**: prick punch 30° (light marking), centre punch 90° (drill start). **Hammers**: ball peen (fitter's), cross peen, straight peen; parts: face, peen, cheek, eye, handle; specified by **weight of the head** (0.45 kg common).
key_points: File parts: tang, heel (shoulder), face, edge, point; length excludes the tang
Classification by cut: single, double, rasp, curved; by grade: rough > bastard > second cut > smooth > dead smooth; by shape: flat, hand, square, round, half round, triangular, knife, needle
Hand file has one safe edge (no teeth) for filing into a corner without cutting the adjacent face
Pinning = metal particles clog the teeth and scratch the job; cleaned with a file card, prevented with chalk
Hacksaw blade 250/300 mm; teeth forward, cut on forward stroke; pitch 14/18/24/32 teeth per 25 mm for soft-thick / general / tube / thin sheet
Set of teeth (alternate, wave) gives kerf clearance
Chisels: flat, cross-cut, half-round, diamond-point; point angle increases with hardness of job
Prick punch 30°, centre punch 90° (some manuals list a 60° dot punch)
Hammer specified by head weight; ball peen for riveting and general fitting
formulas: $p = \dfrac{25.4}{n}$ mm — blade pitch from teeth per inch (25 mm) $n$
teeth in contact $\approx \dfrac{t}{p} \ge 2\text{ to }3$ — section thickness $t$ for choosing pitch
traps: Including the tang in the file length
Fitting the hacksaw blade with teeth towards the handle, or saying it cuts on the return stroke
Listing the grades out of order; bastard is coarser than second cut
Pressing on the return stroke of a file; pressure is on the forward stroke only
Swapping the prick punch (30°) and centre punch (90°) angles
Specifying a hammer by handle length instead of head weight

options: From heel to point, excluding the tang
questions.a: File length is the distance from the heel (shoulder) to the point; the tang is excluded.

questions.q: The correct order of files from coarsest to finest is
options: Rough, second cut, bastard, smooth, dead smooth
Rough, bastard, second cut, smooth, dead smooth
Bastard, rough, smooth, second cut, dead smooth
Dead smooth, smooth, second cut, bastard, rough
questions.a: Rough, bastard, second cut, smooth, dead smooth: teeth get finer and closer in that order.

questions.q: For sawing a thin-walled tube, the hacksaw blade should have about
questions.a: Thin sections need a fine pitch (24, or 32 for very thin sheet) so that at least 2-3 teeth are in contact; a coarse blade straddles the wall and the teeth break.

questions.q: The included point angle of a centre punch is
questions.a: Centre punch 90° makes a wide, deep mark that guides the drill point; the prick punch is 30° for light marking along lines.

questions.q: Classify files according to cut, grade and shape. Sketch a file and name its parts.
questions.a:
**Sketch description:** a long tapering blade; at one end a pointed tang (fitted into a wooden handle), then the heel/shoulder, then the toothed faces and edges along the body, ending in the point/tip.

**Parts:** tang, heel (shoulder), face, edge, point. Length = heel to point.

**By cut:** single cut (one row of parallel teeth at about 60-65°), double cut (overcut + upcut crossing), rasp cut (individual raised teeth, for wood/leather/soft materials), curved cut (soft metals like aluminium).

**By grade:** rough, bastard, second cut, smooth, dead smooth (coarsest to finest; teeth per cm increase).

**By shape:** flat, hand (parallel width, one safe edge), square, round (rat tail), half round, triangular (three square), knife edge, needle (small sets for fine work).

questions.q: What is pinning of a file? How is it prevented and removed?
questions.a: Pinning is the clogging of file teeth by small chips (pins) of the metal being filed, especially soft metals like aluminium. The lodged pins scratch the job and reduce cutting. **Prevention:** rub chalk on the file, use light pressure, use the right cut (single/curved for soft metals). **Removal:** clean the teeth with a file card (wire brush) along the line of the teeth; a pointed soft metal strip lifts stubborn pins.

questions.q: A hacksaw blade has 18 teeth per 25.4 mm. Find its pitch and state whether it is suitable for a 1.5 mm thick sheet.
questions.a:
$$p = \frac{25.4}{18} = 1.41\ \text{mm}$$
Teeth in contact with a 1.5 mm sheet: $t/p = 1.5/1.41 \approx 1.06$, i.e. only about one tooth. The rule needs at least 2-3 teeth, so the blade is **not suitable**: the teeth would straddle the sheet and snap. Use 32 teeth per 25 mm ($p = 0.79$ mm, about 2 teeth) for thin sheet.

questions.q: Sketch a ball peen hammer, name its parts and state how hammers are specified.
questions.a:
**Sketch description:** a forged high carbon steel head with a flat, slightly convex hardened **face** at one end and a hemispherical **ball peen** at the other; the middle portion is the **cheek**, pierced by an oval **eye** into which a wooden (ash/cane) **handle** is fitted and secured with a steel or wooden **wedge**.

**Parts:** face, peen, cheek, eye, wedge, handle. **Specification:** by the weight of the head (e.g. 0.25, 0.45, 0.9 kg). **Uses:** striking chisels and punches (face), riveting and peening (ball).

topics.why: Short 'sketch and use' questions and frequent viva questions; the trick is knowing that calipers are transfer instruments and which caliper does what.
topics.gist:
Calipers and dividers have no scale of their own. A caliper is set to the work and then read against a steel rule (or set from the rule and offered to the work), so they are called **transfer** or **indirect measuring** instruments. Their accuracy is about 0.25 mm and depends on the 'feel' of the user.

- **Outside caliper**: legs bowed inwards; measures outside diameters and thicknesses of bars and plates.
- **Inside caliper**: legs straight with tips turned outwards; measures bore diameters and slot widths.
- **Odd-leg (hermaphrodite, jenny) caliper**: one bent leg and one straight pointed leg; scribes lines parallel to a finished edge and locates the centre of a round bar.
- **Dividers**: two straight legs with hardened, sharp points; scribe circles and arcs, step off equal distances, transfer lengths from a rule.

By construction they are **firm-joint** (legs held by friction at a riveted joint; set by tapping) or **spring-joint** (bow spring, adjusting screw and nut; finer setting, holds its setting). Size is the length from the joint/pivot centre to the tip, e.g. 150 mm.

When calipering, the legs should just touch the work and slide over under their own weight; forcing them springs the legs and gives a wrong reading. Hold the caliper square to the axis.
key_points: Calipers and dividers are transfer (indirect) instruments: no scale, read off a steel rule
Outside caliper: external diameters; inside caliper: bores and slots
Odd-leg caliper: lines parallel to an edge, centre of a round bar
Dividers: circles, arcs, stepping off distances
Firm-joint vs spring-joint construction; spring type holds the setting with a screw and nut
Size = length from pivot to tip (e.g. 150 mm)
Correct feel: the legs just contact and drag lightly; never force
traps: Calling calipers direct-reading instruments
Using dividers to measure a diameter (that is the caliper's job) or odd-leg calipers for a bore
Mixing up the sketches: the outside caliper's legs curve in; the inside caliper's tips turn out

questions.q: Odd-leg calipers are mainly used to
options: Scribe lines parallel to an edge and locate the centre of a bar
questions.a: The hermaphrodite (odd-leg) caliper has one bent leg that rides on the edge and one pointed leg that scribes a parallel line; it also locates the centre of a round bar.

questions.q: Calipers are called transfer instruments because
options: They have no scale; the size is transferred to a steel rule for reading
They are used only for transferring centres
questions.a: A caliper copies the size; the actual value is read by transferring the setting to a steel rule or other scale.

questions.q: The size of a caliper is specified by
options: The length from the joint centre to the tip of the leg
questions.a: Calipers and dividers are specified by leg length from the pivot centre to the tip, e.g. 150 mm.

questions.q: Sketch and describe outside, inside and odd-leg calipers with their uses.
questions.a:
**Outside caliper:** two legs bowed inward (like brackets) meeting at a firm or spring joint; the tips close on the outside of the work. Use: outside diameters, thickness.

**Inside caliper:** two straight legs with the tips turned outwards; the tips open against the walls of a hole. Use: bore diameters, widths of slots and grooves.

**Odd-leg caliper:** one leg bent (stepped) at the tip, the other straight with a scribing point. Use: scribing lines parallel to a finished edge, locating the centre of a round bar's end face.

All three are transfer instruments read against a steel rule; firm-joint or spring-joint types; size by leg length.

questions.q: Differentiate between calipers and dividers.
questions.a:
| Calipers | Dividers |
|---|---|
| Legs bent (outside/inside/odd-leg) | Legs straight with sharp points |
| Used to measure/transfer diameters, thicknesses | Used to scribe circles and arcs, step off distances |
| Tips are blunt contact points | Points are hardened for scribing |
| Measuring (transfer) instrument | Marking instrument |

questions.q: Compare firm-joint and spring-joint calipers.
questions.a: **Firm-joint:** legs held together by friction at a riveted joint; setting changed by tapping a leg lightly; can be opened wide quickly but may lose setting if knocked. **Spring-joint:** legs held by a bow spring at the top, opened/closed by a screw and knurled nut; finer, more reliable setting that does not shift, but slower to change over large ranges.

topics.why: Twist drill nomenclature with the 118° point angle, the taper/second/plug tap set, and the tap-drill-size sum are classic 3-5 mark questions and viva staples.
topics.gist:
**Drilling** makes a round hole with a rotating **twist drill** (HSS, sometimes carbon steel or carbide-tipped) fed axially into the work.

**Twist drill nomenclature:** the **shank** (straight for small drills held in a chuck; **Morse taper** for larger ones, with a **tang** that drives and is used to knock the drill out with a drift), the **body** with two helical **flutes** (carry chips out and coolant in), **land/margin** (narrow strip that keeps the drill aligned and sized), **body clearance**, **web** (central core) ending in the **chisel edge**, and two **lips (cutting edges)**. Standard **point angle 118°** (59° each side) for mild steel, **helix angle** about 30°, **lip clearance angle** 8-12°.

**Tapping** cuts an **internal thread** in a drilled hole. A **tap set** has three taps of the same size: the **taper (first) tap** with a long taper to start the thread, the **second (intermediate) tap**, and the **plug (bottoming) tap** with almost no taper to cut full threads to the bottom of a blind hole. Taps are turned by a **tap wrench**, half a turn forward and a quarter turn back to break the chip, with cutting oil. The hole is first drilled to the **tap drill size**, roughly major diameter minus pitch. External threads are cut by a **die** in a **die stock**.

Reaming finishes a drilled hole to size; counterboring and countersinking open the mouth for bolt heads and screws.

questions.q: Explain the procedure of tapping a hole in a mild steel plate.
questions.a:
1. Mark and centre-punch the hole position.
2. Drill the hole to the tap drill size ($\approx D - p$, e.g. 8.5 mm for M10).
3. Chamfer the mouth slightly.
4. Hold the plate firmly in the vice, hole vertical.
5. Fix the **taper tap** in a tap wrench, place it square in the hole (check with a try square), apply light downward pressure and turn clockwise.
6. After every half turn, turn back a quarter turn to break and clear the chips; apply cutting oil.
7. Follow with the **second tap** and, for blind holes, the **plug (bottoming) tap**.
8. Clean the hole and check with a bolt.

topics.topic: Vernier caliper: principle, least count, reading
topics.why: The guaranteed numerical of the fitting unit: least count from the scale data and a reading with zero-error correction, plus the sketch with parts. Also asked in every viva because it is used on the job.
topics.gist:
A vernier caliper measures to 0.02 mm (or 0.05 / 0.1 mm), far better than a steel rule's 0.5 mm.

**Principle:** two scales with slightly different division sizes. The main scale division (MSD) is, say, 1 mm; on the vernier, n divisions occupy (n − 1) main scale divisions, so each vernier division (VSD) is a little shorter than an MSD. The difference, **1 MSD − 1 VSD**, is the **least count (LC)**, the smallest length the instrument can resolve. With 50 vernier divisions = 49 mm, LC = 1/50 = **0.02 mm**.

**Parts:** main scale on the beam, fixed jaw, movable jaw with the vernier scale, lower jaws for outside measurement, upper (knife-edge) jaws for inside measurement, depth bar (blade) at the end, fine-adjustment screw and clamping screws.

**Reading:** (1) note the main scale reading (MSR) just before the vernier zero; (2) find the vernier division that coincides exactly with any main scale line (VSC); (3) reading = MSR + VSC × LC.

**Zero error:** close the jaws. If the vernier zero lies to the right of the main zero, the error is **positive** (+ VSC × LC) and must be subtracted; if to the left, it is **negative**, equal to −(n − VSC) × LC, and is added. Corrected reading = observed reading − (zero error, with its sign).

Avoid parallax, do not over-tighten the jaws, and measure across the true diameter.
key_points: LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = (value of 1 MSD) / (number of vernier divisions), when n VSD = (n − 1) MSD
Common LCs: 0.1 mm (10 VSD = 9 mm), 0.05 mm (20 VSD = 19 mm), 0.02 mm (50 VSD = 49 mm)
Reading = MSR + VSC × LC
Positive zero error: vernier zero right of main zero; subtract it. Negative: left of main zero; add it
Corrected reading = observed − zero error (with sign)
Parts: beam/main scale, fixed and movable jaws, outside jaws, inside (knife-edge) jaws, depth bar, vernier scale, clamp screw, fine adjustment
Measures outside dimensions, inside dimensions and depth
Sources of error: parallax, excessive pressure, worn jaws, jaws not square to the work
formulas: $LC = 1\ \text{MSD} - 1\ \text{VSD} = \dfrac{s}{n}$ — $s$ = value of one main scale division, $n$ = number of vernier divisions
$\text{Reading} = \text{MSR} + \text{VSC} \times LC$
$\text{Corrected reading} = \text{Observed reading} - (\pm\,\text{zero error})$
$\text{Negative zero error} = -(n - \text{VSC}) \times LC$
traps: Taking LC as MSD / (n − 1) instead of MSD / n
Adding a positive zero error instead of subtracting it
Reading the main scale at the nearest line instead of the line just before the vernier zero
For an extended vernier (e.g. 20 VSD = 39 MSD) LC is 2 MSD − 1 VSD; do not use s/n blindly
Writing the result without units or with the wrong number of decimals (LC 0.02 gives two decimals)

questions.a: $LC = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = 1 - \tfrac{49}{50} = \tfrac{1}{50} = 0.02$ mm.

questions.q: When the jaws of a vernier caliper are closed, the vernier zero lies to the right of the main scale zero. The zero error is
options: Positive, and is added to the reading
Positive, and is subtracted from the reading
Negative, and is added to the reading
Negative, and is subtracted from the reading
questions.a: Vernier zero to the right means the instrument reads more than zero with nothing between the jaws: a positive error, which is subtracted from every observed reading.

questions.q: Explain the principle of a vernier caliper. A main scale is graduated in mm and 50 vernier divisions equal 49 mm. Find the least count and the reading when the main scale reading is 42 mm and the 23rd vernier division coincides.
questions.a:
**Principle:** the vernier works on the difference between two scales. $n$ vernier divisions are made equal to $(n-1)$ main scale divisions, so each VSD is shorter than an MSD by a small fixed amount, the least count. When the jaws open by a fraction of an MSD, the vernier line that coincides with a main scale line tells how many least counts that fraction is.

**Least count:** $1\text{ VSD} = 49/50 = 0.98$ mm
$$LC = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = 1 - 0.98 = 0.02\ \text{mm}$$

**Reading:**
$$= \text{MSR} + \text{VSC} \times LC = 42 + 23 \times 0.02 = 42 + 0.46 = 42.46\ \text{mm}$$

questions.q: A vernier caliper of least count 0.02 mm (50 vernier divisions) shows the following with the jaws closed: the vernier zero is to the right of the main scale zero and the 4th vernier division coincides. A rod then reads MSR = 25 mm with the 36th division coinciding. Find the true diameter.
questions.a:
Zero error $= +4 \times 0.02 = +0.08$ mm (positive, vernier zero to the right).

Observed reading $= 25 + 36 \times 0.02 = 25 + 0.72 = 25.72$ mm.

Corrected reading $= 25.72 - (+0.08) = 25.64$ mm.

**True diameter = 25.64 mm.**

questions.q: With the jaws closed, the vernier zero of a 0.02 mm caliper (50 divisions) is to the left of the main zero and the 46th vernier division coincides. A job reads MSR 18 mm and VSC 12. Find the corrected reading.
questions.a:
Vernier zero to the left: negative zero error.
$$\text{Zero error} = -(n - \text{VSC}) \times LC = -(50 - 46) \times 0.02 = -0.08\ \text{mm}$$
Observed reading $= 18 + 12 \times 0.02 = 18.24$ mm.
Corrected $= 18.24 - (-0.08) = 18.32$ mm.

questions.q: The main scale of a vernier caliper has divisions of 0.5 mm, and 25 vernier divisions coincide with 24 main scale divisions. Find the least count.
questions.a:
$1\text{ MSD} = 0.5$ mm; $1\text{ VSD} = \frac{24 \times 0.5}{25} = 0.48$ mm.
$$LC = 0.5 - 0.48 = 0.02\ \text{mm}$$
(equivalently $LC = s/n = 0.5/25 = 0.02$ mm)

questions.q: Sketch a vernier caliper and name its parts. What three kinds of measurement can it make?
questions.a:
**Sketch description:** a long flat **beam** engraved with the **main scale**; at the left end the **fixed jaw** (lower, for outside measurement) with a small upper knife-edge jaw; a **sliding head/movable jaw** carrying the **vernier scale**, its own lower outside jaw and upper inside jaw, a **clamping (locking) screw** and often a **fine-adjustment** unit; a thin **depth bar** projecting from the right end of the beam, moving with the slider.

**Measurements:** (1) outside dimensions with the lower jaws, (2) inside dimensions (bores, slots) with the upper knife-edge jaws, (3) depths of holes and steps with the depth bar.

questions.q: List four precautions while using a vernier caliper.
questions.a:
1. Check and note the zero error before measuring.
2. Read with the eye directly over the coinciding lines (avoid parallax).
3. Apply light, uniform pressure; do not force the jaws or measure a rotating or hot job.
4. Hold the jaws square to the axis / across the true diameter; clean the jaws and work; lock the slider before removing the caliper.

topics.why: Paired with the vernier as the standard measurement numerical: least count from pitch and thimble divisions, a reading with the half-millimetre line, and zero error. Sketch with parts is a frequent 5-marker.
topics.gist:
The **outside micrometer (screw gauge)** measures to **0.01 mm**.

**Principle: screw and nut.** When a screw turns one full revolution in a fixed nut, it advances axially by one **pitch**. If the thimble attached to the screw is divided into n equal divisions, turning it by one division advances the spindle by pitch/n. That is the **least count**: with pitch 0.5 mm and 50 thimble divisions, LC = 0.5/50 = **0.01 mm**.

**Parts:** U-shaped **frame** (drop-forged steel, often with heat-insulating pads), **anvil** (fixed measuring face), **spindle** (moving measuring face, carbide-tipped), **sleeve / barrel** with the datum (reference) line and the main scale in mm above and half mm below the line, **thimble** with the circular scale, **ratchet stop** (gives the same measuring pressure every time; it slips when the faces touch the work), and the **lock nut / spindle lock**. Range is 25 mm: 0-25, 25-50 mm and so on.

**Reading:** sleeve reading (whole mm plus 0.5 mm if the half mark is visible) + thimble division on the datum line × LC.

**Zero error:** with the faces touching (or on the setting standard for the 25-50 size), if the thimble zero has passed below the datum line and division x sits on it, error = +x × LC (subtract); if the zero has not reached the line and division x sits on it, error = −(n − x) × LC (add).

A vernier micrometer adds a vernier on the sleeve and reads 0.001 mm.

LC = pitch / number of thimble divisions = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm
Parts: frame, anvil, spindle, sleeve/barrel with datum line, thimble, ratchet stop, lock nut
Ratchet stop ensures constant measuring pressure
Reading = sleeve reading (including the 0.5 mm line) + thimble reading × LC
Range is 25 mm per micrometer (0-25, 25-50, ...)
Positive zero error: thimble zero below the datum line; negative: above it
Inside, depth, screw-thread and vernier micrometers are variants
formulas: $LC = \dfrac{\text{pitch}}{\text{number of thimble divisions}} = \dfrac{0.5}{50} = 0.01$ mm
$\text{Reading} = \text{sleeve reading} + \text{thimble division} \times LC$
$\text{Negative zero error} = -(n - x) \times LC$ — when division $x$ is on the datum line before zero
traps: Missing the half-millimetre line on the lower side of the sleeve: reading 7.28 instead of 7.78
Taking pitch as 1 mm by default; read the pitch from the data
Turning the thimble directly to tighten instead of using the ratchet
Thinking a micrometer measures 0-150 mm like a vernier; each one covers 25 mm

questions.a: A screw advancing in a nut by one pitch per revolution; subdividing the revolution on the thimble gives fine readings.

questions.q: A 0-25 mm micrometer (pitch 0.5 mm, 50 thimble divisions) shows 7 mm on the sleeve with the half-millimetre line visible, and the 28th thimble division on the datum line. Find the reading.
questions.a:
$LC = 0.5/50 = 0.01$ mm.

Sleeve reading $= 7 + 0.5 = 7.5$ mm.

Thimble reading $= 28 \times 0.01 = 0.28$ mm.

$$\text{Reading} = 7.5 + 0.28 = 7.78\ \text{mm}$$

questions.a:
Zero not yet reached: negative zero error.
$$e = -(50 - 47) \times 0.01 = -0.03\ \text{mm}$$
Observed $= 3.5 + 12 \times 0.01 = 3.62$ mm.
Corrected $= 3.62 - (-0.03) = 3.65$ mm.

questions.q: Explain the principle and construction of an outside micrometer with a sketch description.
questions.a:
**Principle:** a screw turning in a fixed nut advances axially by one pitch per revolution. Dividing the circumference of the thimble into $n$ parts lets the advance be read to pitch/$n$: $LC = 0.5/50 = 0.01$ mm.

**Sketch description:** a U-shaped frame; on the left arm the fixed **anvil**; on the right arm the **barrel/sleeve**, inside which is the precision-threaded **spindle** whose face meets the anvil. The **thimble**, fixed to the spindle, slides over the sleeve. The sleeve carries a longitudinal **datum line** with mm graduations above and 0.5 mm graduations below; the thimble's bevelled edge carries 50 divisions. A **ratchet stop** at the end of the thimble and a **lock nut** on the frame complete it.

**Use:** place the work between anvil and spindle, close with the ratchet until it clicks, lock, read sleeve + thimble × LC, correct for zero error.

questions.q: Compare the vernier caliper and the micrometer.
questions.a:
| Vernier caliper | Micrometer |
|---|---|
| Vernier principle (difference of two scales) | Screw and nut principle |
| LC usually 0.02 mm | LC usually 0.01 mm |
| Range large (0-150/300 mm) in one instrument | 25 mm range per instrument |
| Measures outside, inside and depth | Separate outside, inside, depth micrometers |
| No constant-pressure device; feel-dependent | Ratchet gives uniform pressure |
| Faster, more versatile | More accurate, follows Abbe's principle (measuring axis in line with scale) |

topics.why: Short questions on use and construction and a vernier-type reading; the reading method is the same as the caliper, so it is cheap marks.
topics.gist:
Both gauges use the **same vernier principle** as the vernier caliper, usually with **LC 0.02 mm**, and are read the same way: MSR + VSC × LC, corrected for zero error.

The **vernier height gauge** stands on a **surface plate**. It has a heavy, hardened, ground **base**, a vertical **beam** carrying the main scale, a **slider** carrying the vernier with a fine-adjustment screw and clamp, and a **measuring jaw** to which a **scriber** (or a dial indicator) is clamped. Uses: measuring the height of a face or step above the surface plate, and, more often in the fitting shop, **precise marking out**: set the scriber at the required height and slide the gauge so the scriber marks a line parallel to the datum. Zero is checked by lowering the jaw on to the surface plate. It is the precise version of the surface gauge.

The **vernier depth gauge** has a **base (stock)** with a flat, wide reference face that bridges the hole or slot, and a narrow graduated **beam/rod** that slides through it, with the vernier on the base. Uses: depths of blind holes, slots, recesses and steps. Hold the base firmly flat across the mouth, push the beam lightly until it touches the bottom, lock and read. Zero is checked by standing the base and beam end together on a surface plate.

Height gauge: base, beam with main scale, slider with vernier, fine adjustment, measuring jaw with scriber
Height gauge is used on a surface plate for measuring heights and precision marking
Depth gauge: base/stock bridging the hole, sliding beam, vernier, clamp screw
Depth gauge measures depths of blind holes, slots, steps
Zero is checked on a surface plate for both
Reading = MSR + VSC × LC, minus zero error

Confusing the height gauge with the surface gauge, which has no scale
Rocking the depth gauge base or letting the beam push it up off the surface

questions.q: Describe the construction and uses of a vernier height gauge.
questions.a:
**Construction (sketch description):** a heavy hardened and ground **base** that sits on the surface plate; a vertical **beam** fixed to it with the **main scale** engraved; a **slider** carrying the **vernier scale**, with a **clamping screw** and a **fine-adjustment** screw and nut; a **measuring jaw** projecting from the slider, to which a hardened **scriber** (or a dial test indicator) is clamped.

**Uses:** (1) measuring the height of steps, faces and hole centres above the surface plate; (2) precision marking: set the scriber to the required height and slide the base along the plate so the scriber scribes a line parallel to the datum; (3) with a dial indicator, comparing heights and checking parallelism.

**Reading:** same as the vernier caliper, LC usually 0.02 mm; check zero on the plate first.

questions.q: How is a vernier depth gauge used? State two precautions.
questions.a: Place the base flat across the mouth of the hole or slot, hold it down firmly, slide the beam down until its end just touches the bottom, lock the clamp screw, remove and read MSR + VSC × LC (minus zero error). **Precautions:** (1) keep the base pressed flat; do not let the beam lift it; (2) clean the hole bottom and gauge faces, check zero on a surface plate, and read without parallax.

topics.topic: Fitting processes: marking, chipping, sawing, filing
topics.why: Questions ask for the operations and the sequence of making the shop job (square, T, V or dovetail fit), and the viva is entirely about how you made it.
topics.gist:
**Fitting** is making parts by hand so that they assemble with the required clearance. The shop job (square fit, T-fit, V-fit, dovetail) uses all four basic processes.

**Marking:** check the stock size, file two adjacent edges flat and square as **datum (reference) edges**, coat with chalk/copper sulphate, mark all lines from the datum with a height gauge or try square and scriber, and put **witness marks** with a prick punch along the lines (half the dot should remain after filing). Centre-punch hole centres.

**Chipping:** removing metal with a cold chisel and ball peen hammer; hold the chisel at about 35-40° to the surface, watch the cutting edge not the chisel head, wear goggles, use a chipping screen.

**Sawing:** hold the job low in the vice with the line close to the jaws, start the cut with a nick from a file, cut on the forward stroke at about 40-50 strokes per minute using the full length of the blade, light pressure on the return. Saw in the waste, about 1 mm from the line.

**Filing:** **cross (straight) filing** for fast removal, **draw filing** (file held at both ends, moved sideways along the work) for a fine finish, pressure only on the forward stroke, feet apart, file kept level (avoid rocking, which makes the surface convex). Check with a try square and steel rule against light.

Then drilling, tapping and final fitting, deburring and checking dimensions with the vernier.
key_points: Fitting = making and assembling parts by hand to the required fit
Sequence: check stock, file datum edges square, mark, punch, saw off waste, file to line, drill/tap, finish, check
Witness marks with a prick punch: half the dot left after filing shows you filed to the line
Chipping: cold chisel at 35-40°, eye on the cutting edge, goggles
Sawing: forward stroke cuts, 40-50 strokes/min, full blade length, cut in the waste
Cross filing for removal, draw filing for finish; pressure on forward stroke only
Rocking the file gives a convex surface; check flatness with a try square against light
Deburr every edge before measuring and assembling
traps: Not mentioning datum edges; everything is marked from two finished edges at 90°
Writing that you saw on the line; you saw in the waste and file to the line
Pressure on the return stroke, or file not lifted on the return
Leaving out safety (goggles in chipping, no loose sleeves, no handle-less file)

questions.a: In draw filing the file is held at both ends and pushed and pulled sideways along the work, giving a fine finish.

questions.a: Rocking removes more at the edges than at the middle, so the surface becomes convex.

questions.a: Teeth point forward; pressure on the forward stroke, relieved on the return.

questions.q: Write the sequence of operations for making a square (male-female) fit from two mild steel plates.
questions.a:
1. Check the raw stock with a steel rule.
2. File two adjacent edges of each plate flat and at 90° (datum edges); check with a try square.
3. File the other edges to the overall size.
4. Apply chalk/copper sulphate; mark the male and female profiles from the datum edges with a height gauge/try square and scriber.
5. Prick-punch witness marks along the lines; centre-punch and drill relief holes at internal corners.
6. Hacksaw the waste about 1 mm from the lines.
7. File to the lines (rough then smooth file), checking squareness and size with a try square and vernier.
8. Try the male in the female; ease high spots by filing.
9. Deburr, finish with draw filing, clean and check final dimensions.

questions.q: Describe the chipping operation and its safety precautions.
questions.a: Chipping removes surplus metal with a cold chisel struck by a ball peen hammer. The job is held firmly in the vice with the cut towards the fixed jaw; the chisel is held at about 35-40° to the surface (the clearance gives the depth of cut), and struck with steady blows while the eye follows the cutting edge. Light finishing cuts follow heavy cuts, and the last chip is taken from the other side to avoid breaking the edge. **Safety:** goggles, chipping screen, mushroom-headed chisels dressed/ground, firm grip, hammer handle secure.

questions.q: Distinguish cross filing and draw filing.
questions.a: **Cross (straight) filing:** the file is pushed forward across the work, often in two crossing directions, with the handle in one hand and the point in the other; used for rapid metal removal and flattening. **Draw filing:** the file is held at both ends at right angles to the work and moved along its length; removes little metal, used to give a smooth, straight-grained finish on narrow surfaces and edges.

questions.q: Why are witness marks made, and how much of the dot should remain after filing?
questions.a: Witness marks are prick-punch dots along the scribed line, because a scribed line rubs off easily. When filing, you file down to the dots until exactly half of each dot remains: proof that the edge is on the line. If whole dots remain you are short of the line; if none remain you have gone past it.

topics.why: 'Classify welding processes' is a standard 5-mark question in the mid and end term; fusion vs pressure and welding vs brazing vs soldering are frequent short answers.
topics.gist:
**Welding** is joining two metal pieces by heating them to a suitable temperature, with or without pressure and with or without filler metal, so that they **coalesce** into one piece.

**Classification by the state of the metal:**
- **Fusion (non-pressure) welding**: the edges are melted, filler usually added, no pressure. Gas welding (oxy-acetylene, about 3200 °C for the neutral flame), arc welding (shielded metal arc / SMAW, carbon arc, TIG/GTAW, MIG/GMAW, submerged arc, plasma arc), thermit welding, electron beam and laser welding.
- **Pressure (plastic) welding**: the metal is heated only to a plastic state (or not at all) and forced together. Forge welding, resistance welding (spot, seam, projection, butt, flash), and **solid-state** processes such as friction, ultrasonic, explosive and diffusion welding (pressure, no melting).

**Classification by heat source:** gas (chemical flame), electric arc, electrical resistance ($H = I^2 R t$), chemical reaction (thermit: Al + iron oxide), friction, radiant energy (laser, electron beam).

**Allied processes:** **brazing** (filler above 450 °C, below the base metal's melting point, e.g. brass/silver alloys) and **soldering** (filler below 450 °C, e.g. Sn-Pb); in both the base metal is **not melted** and the filler is drawn in by capillary action. Welding is the only one of the three in which the base metal melts (in fusion welding) and the joint is usually as strong as the parent metal.

topics.why: Short questions on weld joints, weld zones (fusion zone, HAZ) and nomenclature (root, toe, throat) appear; the fillet-throat relation gives an easy numerical.
topics.gist:
A **weld** is the localised union of two metal parts produced by heat (and/or pressure), with the joint metallurgically continuous with the parent metal. Three regions form across it:

1. **Fusion zone (weld metal)**: metal that melted and solidified, a mix of filler and base metal, with a cast (columnar) structure.
2. **Heat-affected zone (HAZ)**: base metal not melted but heated enough to change its grain structure and properties (grain growth, hardening in steels). This is where cracks often start.
3. **Unaffected base (parent) metal.**

**Types of joints** (the relative position of the plates): **butt, lap, tee (T), corner and edge**.

**Types of welds** (the shape of the deposit): **fillet** (triangular section in lap, T and corner joints), **groove/butt** (square, single V, double V, single U, J, bevel; edges prepared on plates over about 5-6 mm so the arc penetrates), plug, slot, spot and seam welds.

**Nomenclature:** **root** (where the members are closest), **face** (exposed surface), **toe** (junction of face and base metal), **reinforcement** (metal above the plate surface), **penetration** (depth of fusion), **leg** and **throat** of a fillet (throat = 0.707 × leg for an equal-leg fillet).

**Welding positions:** flat (1G/1F), horizontal (2G/2F), vertical (3G/3F), overhead (4G/4F). Flat is easiest; overhead the hardest.

2. **Lap joint**: one plate overlapping the other, fillet welds along the edges.
3. **Tee joint**: one plate perpendicular to the other at its middle, like a T, fillet welds on one or both sides.
4. **Corner joint**: two plates meeting at their edges at 90°, forming an L corner.
5. **Edge joint**: two plates placed face to face with edges flush, weld along the edges.

questions.a:

Shear area $= t \times l = 5.656 \times 100 = 565.6$ mm².

$$P = 0.707\, s\, l\, \tau = 565.6 \times 80 = 45{,}248\ \text{N} \approx 45.2\ \text{kN}$$

questions.q: Sketch a butt weld and a fillet weld and mark the root, face, toe, reinforcement, penetration, leg and throat.
questions.a:
**Butt (single V) weld:** two plates with bevelled edges forming a V; the bottom where they nearly meet is the **root**; the bead filling the V bulges above the plate as **reinforcement**; its exposed surface is the **face**; the lines where the face meets the plate surface are the **toes**; the depth to which fusion reaches into the plates is the **penetration**.

**Fillet weld:** a triangular bead in the corner of a T/lap joint; the two sides along the plates are the **legs** ($s$); the shortest distance from the root to the hypotenuse is the **throat** ($t = 0.707s$); the junctions of the bead face with the plates are the **toes**; the corner is the **root**.

questions.q: What are the four welding positions? Which is the easiest and why?
questions.a: Flat (1G/1F), horizontal (2G/2F), vertical (3G/3F) and overhead (4G/4F). Flat is easiest because gravity holds the molten pool in the joint, allowing higher current, faster deposition and better penetration; overhead is the hardest because the pool tends to drip.

topics.why: 'Explain the principle of arc welding with a neat sketch' is close to certain in the end term, with polarity (DCSP/DCRP) and arc length as follow-ups.
topics.gist:
In **electric arc welding** the heat comes from an **electric arc**, a sustained discharge through ionised gas between the **electrode** and the **workpiece**. The electrode is connected to one terminal of the power source and the work (through the earth clamp) to the other.

**Striking the arc:** the electrode is touched to the work (by **scratching** or **tapping**), which short-circuits and heats the contact spot, then withdrawn to a gap of about **2-4 mm** (roughly equal to the electrode core diameter). Electrons emitted from the hot cathode ionise the air; the arc forms and its temperature reaches about **5000-6000 °C** (textbooks quote 3500-6000 °C). This melts the work edges and the tip of the consumable electrode; metal drops transfer across the arc to the weld pool.

In SMAW (manual metal arc) the electrode coating burns to give a **gas shield** and a **slag** layer that protect the pool from oxygen and nitrogen and slow its cooling. Slag is chipped off after cooling.

**Electrical values:** open-circuit voltage about **50-90 V** (AC sets about 70-100 V); arc voltage **20-40 V**; current **50-500 A** depending on electrode size.

**Polarity (DC):** about two-thirds of the heat is released at the positive pole (classical textbook figure). **DCSP / DCEN** (electrode negative, work positive): more heat in the work, **deep penetration**, thick plates. **DCRP / DCEP** (electrode positive): more heat in the electrode, faster melting, **shallow penetration**, thin sheets and non-ferrous metals. With AC, heat is shared equally.

questions.a:
**Sketch description:** a welding transformer/generator with two output cables; one goes to the **electrode holder** gripping a coated **electrode**, the other to the **earth (ground) clamp** on the **workpiece** lying on the welding table. Between the electrode tip and the work is the **arc**, below it the **molten weld pool**, behind it the solidified **bead** covered by **slag**, and around the arc the **gaseous shield** from the burning coating.

**Principle:** when the electrode touches the work and is withdrawn 2-4 mm, current continues through the ionised air gap as an arc. Electron bombardment converts electrical energy to heat, about 5000-6000 °C, which melts the base metal edges and the electrode tip. Molten drops from the electrode transfer to the pool; on cooling, the pool solidifies into a weld bead joining the pieces. The flux coating stabilises the arc, shields the pool from atmospheric O₂ and N₂, deoxidises the metal and forms slag that slows cooling.

**Typical values:** OCV 50-90 V, arc voltage 20-40 V, current 50-500 A; AC or DC.

topics.why: 'What is arc blow? State its causes and remedies' is a favourite 3-5 mark question and viva question, often linked to why AC is preferred.
topics.gist:
**Arc blow** is the **deflection of the arc from its intended path**, so it wanders forwards, backwards or sideways instead of going straight from the electrode tip into the joint. It is a problem mainly with **DC welding**.

**Cause:** the welding current produces a magnetic field around the electrode, the arc and the workpiece. In the plate, the current path and the shape of the steel make this field **unsymmetrical**: the lines of force crowd where the magnetic material ends, at the **ends of joints, edges, corners and near the earth connection**. The arc, being a current-carrying conductor, is pushed away from the side where flux is concentrated. **Forward blow** (in the direction of travel) occurs near the start/earth side, **back blow** (opposite to travel) near the end of a joint. Residual magnetism in the plates, high currents and thick, magnetic materials make it worse. With AC the field reverses 100 times a second, so arc blow is negligible.

**Effects:** unstable arc, excessive spatter, incomplete fusion and poor penetration, undercut, porosity, slag inclusions, uneven bead.

**Remedies:** switch to **AC**; hold a **short arc**; **reduce current**; **change the position of the earth (ground) clamp** (or use two earths), welding away from it or towards a heavy tack; **tilt the electrode** to counter the blow; weld towards a heavy tack or already-made weld; use a **back-step** sequence; use run-on and run-off tabs at the joint ends; wrap the earth cable around the work to oppose the field; demagnetise the work.

Mostly a DC problem; negligible with AC because the field reverses
Worst at ends of joints, corners, edges, near the earth clamp, thick magnetic plates, high current

Saying AC causes arc blow; AC is the cure
Listing remedies without the cause (magnetic field asymmetry) loses marks in a 5-mark answer

questions.q: What is arc blow? Explain its causes, effects and remedies.
questions.a:
**Definition:** arc blow is the deflection of the welding arc from its intended path (forward, backward or sideways) due to magnetic forces.

**Causes:** the current in the electrode, arc and work sets up magnetic fields. In a steel plate the flux is unevenly distributed, crowding at the ends of the joint, edges, corners and near the earth connection, and around thick magnetic sections or residual magnetism. The arc is pushed away from the region of concentrated flux. Forward blow occurs near the start (earth side), back blow near the end of the joint. It is serious with DC and high current; negligible with AC.

**Effects:** unstable, wandering arc; spatter; lack of fusion and penetration; undercut; porosity; slag inclusion; irregular bead.

**Remedies:**
1. Use AC.
2. Hold a short arc and reduce current.
3. Change the location of the earth clamp; use two earth connections; weld away from the earth or towards a heavy tack.
4. Incline the electrode against the direction of blow.
5. Use back-step welding and heavy tack welds; weld towards a completed weld.
6. Use run-on/run-off tabs at the ends.
7. Wrap the earth cable around the work; demagnetise the work.

questions.q: Why is arc blow negligible in AC welding?
questions.a: In AC the current, and therefore the magnetic field around the arc, reverses direction every half cycle (100 times a second on 50 Hz). The deflecting force also reverses before the arc can be pushed far, and induced eddy currents in the plate oppose the field, so the net deflection averages to nearly zero.

questions.q: Distinguish forward blow and back blow.
questions.a: **Forward blow:** the arc is deflected ahead in the direction of travel; occurs near the start of the joint / when welding away from the earth; causes shallow penetration and slag running ahead. **Back blow:** the arc is deflected backward over the deposited metal; occurs near the end of the joint / when welding towards the earth; causes undercut and porosity. Changing the earth position or welding direction converts or reduces them.

topics.why: Listing and sketching the equipment and safety gear is a common 3-5 mark question and an easy viva; duty cycle occasionally appears as a numerical.
topics.gist:
A manual metal arc welding station needs:

**1. Power source.**
- **AC welding transformer**: a step-down transformer converting mains (230/415 V) to a low-voltage, high-current supply (OCV 70-100 V); current set by a tapped or movable-core arrangement. Cheap, simple, efficient.
- **DC sources**: **motor-generator** or engine-driven generator (used on site, no mains needed), **rectifier** (transformer + silicon diode bridge), and modern **inverter** sets (light, efficient, stable arc).
- For manual welding the source has a **drooping (constant-current) characteristic**: changes in arc length change voltage a lot but current only a little.
- **Duty cycle**: the percentage of a 10-minute period for which the set can deliver its rated current without overheating (e.g. 60% at 300 A).

**2. Welding cables** (flexible copper/aluminium, heavily insulated): the electrode cable and the earth/ground cable.
**3. Electrode holder**: insulated jaws that grip the bare end of the electrode.
**4. Earth (ground) clamp** on the work or table.
**5. Electrodes.**
**6. Accessories:** chipping hammer (removing slag), wire brush, tongs, welding table, C-clamps, fixtures.
**7. Protective equipment:** **helmet or hand shield** with **filter glass** (shade about 10-12 for 100-300 A) to stop ultraviolet and infrared rays, leather **gloves**, **apron**, sleeves, safety shoes, screens for neighbours, exhaust ventilation.

topics.why: 'Compare AC and DC welding' as a table is one of the most predictable questions of the welding unit, for 3-5 marks.
topics.gist:
Both AC and DC are used for arc welding; the choice depends on cost, material, thickness and position.

**AC welding** uses a transformer: low first cost, almost no maintenance (no moving parts), high efficiency (about 80-85%), no **arc blow** problem, and it can weld thick sections with large electrodes. But the arc is less stable (the current passes through zero 100 times a second), only **coated electrodes** can be used (the coating keeps the arc ionised), polarity cannot be chosen, it is less suited to thin sheet and many non-ferrous metals, the **power factor is low** (about 0.3-0.4), and the higher OCV (70-100 V) means more shock risk.

**DC welding** uses a generator, rectifier or inverter: the arc is **stable**, easy to strike and good in all positions; both **bare and coated electrodes** work; **polarity can be selected** (DCSP for deep penetration, DCRP for thin sheet and non-ferrous); OCV is lower (50-90 V), so it is safer. Its drawbacks are a higher first cost, maintenance of generators, lower efficiency for motor-generator sets (roughly 30-60%), and **arc blow**.

Rule of thumb: AC for heavy mild steel fabrication in the shop; DC for thin sheet, non-ferrous and alloy steels, overhead/vertical work and site work with engine-driven sets.
key_points: AC: transformer, cheap, low maintenance, efficiency ~80-85%, no arc blow, only coated electrodes, low power factor, OCV 70-100 V
DC: generator/rectifier/inverter, costlier, stable arc, polarity choice, bare or coated electrodes, OCV 50-90 V, arc blow
DC better for thin sheet, non-ferrous, out-of-position welding
AC better for thick mild steel with large electrodes where arc blow would be a problem
Heat with AC is equally divided between electrode and work
Engine-driven DC sets work where there is no mains supply
traps: Saying DC has no arc blow; it is the DC side that suffers from it
Saying bare electrodes work on AC; the arc extinguishes at each current zero without the coating's ionising agents
Claiming AC is safer; its higher OCV makes shock more dangerous

questions.q: Why can bare electrodes not be used with AC?
questions.a: With AC the current falls to zero 100 times a second (50 Hz), and the arc momentarily extinguishes. A bare electrode gives nothing to keep the gap ionised, so the arc does not re-strike reliably. Coated electrodes contain ionising elements (potassium, sodium, titanium compounds) that keep the arc path conductive through each zero.

topics.why: Functions of the flux coating, the coating constituents, electrode coding (E6013, E7018) and selection factors are set almost every year for 3-5 marks.
topics.gist:
Electrodes are **consumable** (melt and become filler: the coated electrodes of SMAW, MIG wire) or **non-consumable** (carbon, graphite, tungsten in TIG; filler added separately).

Consumable electrodes are **bare**, **lightly coated** or **heavily coated (shielded)**. A coated electrode is a mild steel **core wire** (1.6-6.3 mm diameter, 250-450 mm long) covered with flux, leaving about 25 mm bare at one end for the holder. **Size = core wire diameter.**

**Functions of the coating:** (1) stabilises the arc (ionising agents) and makes AC possible, (2) produces a **gas shield** that keeps O₂ and N₂ out, (3) forms **slag** that protects the hot bead and slows cooling, (4) **deoxidises** and refines the weld metal, (5) adds **alloying elements**, (6) controls bead shape and allows positional welding, (7) iron powder raises deposition rate.

**Constituents:** rutile, cellulose, CaCO₃/CaF₂, Fe-Mn/Fe-Si (deoxidisers), iron powder, silicate **binder**.

**AWS coding E XX Y Z:** E = electrode; first two (or three) digits = minimum tensile strength in **ksi** (60 → 60,000 psi ≈ 414 MPa; 70 → ≈ 483 MPa); next digit = position (1 = all positions, 2 = flat and horizontal fillet); last digit (with the one before) = coating type and current. **E6013**: rutile-potassium, AC or DC either polarity, general purpose. **E7018**: low-hydrogen iron powder, AC or DCEP.

**Selection depends on:** base metal composition, thickness and joint design, welding position, AC/DC and polarity available, required mechanical properties, and penetration and deposition required. Current is roughly **35-40 A per mm** of core diameter.

questions.q: What are the functions of the flux coating on an arc welding electrode?
questions.a:
1. **Arc stabilisation**: ionising compounds (K, Na, Ti) keep the arc steady and allow AC.
2. **Gas shielding**: burning coating forms CO₂/CO/H₂ that excludes atmospheric O₂ and N₂.
3. **Slag formation**: a slag covers the bead, protects it from oxidation and slows cooling (less brittle weld).
4. **Deoxidation and refining**: Fe-Mn, Fe-Si remove oxygen; impurities float into slag.
5. **Alloying**: adds Mn, Cr, Ni, Mo to the weld metal.
6. **Bead control**: controls penetration, bead shape and fluidity, allowing vertical and overhead welding.
7. **Higher deposition**: iron powder adds metal.
8. **Insulation**: the coating insulates the electrode side, preventing side arcing in narrow joints.

questions.q: Explain the designations E6013 and E7018.
questions.a:
**E6013:** E = electrode for arc welding; 60 = minimum tensile strength 60 ksi (≈ 414 MPa); 1 = usable in all positions; 3 = high-titania (rutile) potassium coating, AC or DC either polarity. A general-purpose, easy-to-use electrode for mild steel fabrication.

**E7018:** 70 ksi (≈ 483 MPa); 1 = all positions; 8 = low-hydrogen potassium coating with iron powder, AC or DCEP. Used for critical, crack-sensitive and thicker structural work; must be kept dry (baked).

questions.q: Select a suitable current for a 3.15 mm electrode using the rule of thumb, and state the factors that govern electrode selection.
questions.a:
**Current:** $I \approx 35\text{-}40 \times 3.15 \approx 110\text{-}126$ A, so about 110-125 A (the manufacturer's range for 3.15 mm rutile is roughly 90-130 A).

**Selection factors:**
1. Composition of the base metal (match strength and chemistry).
2. Thickness and joint design (penetration needed; electrode diameter).
3. Welding position (all-position electrodes for vertical/overhead).
4. Type of current and polarity available (AC/DC).
5. Required mechanical properties (toughness, crack resistance → low-hydrogen).
6. Deposition rate and productivity; fit-up and service conditions.

questions.q: Differentiate consumable and non-consumable electrodes with examples.
questions.a: **Consumable:** melts in the arc and becomes part of the weld as filler metal; must be replaced as it is used up. Examples: coated mild steel electrodes in SMAW, MIG wire, submerged arc wire. **Non-consumable:** does not melt (or melts very slowly); only maintains the arc, filler is added separately if needed. Examples: tungsten (TIG), carbon and graphite electrodes (carbon arc).

topics.why: 'Name and sketch carpentry tools by category' is a standard 5-mark question, and the rip saw vs crosscut saw and jack plane parts are favourites.
topics.gist:
Carpentry tools are grouped by job:

**Marking and measuring:** steel rule and tape, **try square** (wooden or steel stock), **marking gauge** (one pin, lines parallel to an edge along the grain), **mortise gauge** (two pins, marks both sides of a mortise), **bevel square** (any angle), wing compass, scriber/marking knife, pencil.

**Cutting (saws):** the **rip saw** (cuts along the grain; teeth shaped like chisels, about 3-5 points per 25 mm), the **crosscut saw** (across the grain; knife-like teeth, about 6-8 points per 25 mm), the **tenon / back saw** (stiffened back, fine teeth, about 12-14 points, for joints), the **dovetail saw**, **compass and keyhole saws** (curves and internal cuts), the **coping saw** (curves in thin wood).

**Planing:** **jack plane** (the general plane, about 350-400 mm long; parts: body/sole, mouth, cutting iron (blade) at about 45°, cap iron/back iron, lever cap, adjusting nut and lateral lever, handle, knob), **smoothing plane** (short, final finish), **try / jointer plane** (long, true long edges), **rebate plane**, **plough plane**.

**Boring:** gimlet and bradawl (small holes), **brace and bit**, auger, hand drill.

**Chisels:** **firmer** (general), **bevel-edge / paring** (fine paring, dovetails), **mortise chisel** (thick, for chopping mortises).

**Striking:** **claw hammer** (drives and pulls nails), **mallet** (wooden; strikes chisel handles without splitting them).

**Holding:** **carpenter's vice**, bench hook, bar clamp (sash cramp), G-clamp. **Miscellaneous:** screwdriver, pincers, rasp, oilstone for sharpening.

Striking a wooden-handled chisel with a steel hammer instead of a mallet
Mixing the marking gauge (one spur) with the mortise gauge (two spurs)
Forgetting the cap iron's role in the jack plane

**Sketch description:** a long body (wood or cast iron, ~350-400 mm) with a flat **sole**; a slot (**mouth**) across the sole; the **cutting iron (blade)** bedded on the **frog** at about 45°, its edge just projecting through the mouth; the **cap iron (back iron)** screwed to the top of the blade with its edge about 1-2 mm behind the cutting edge; a **lever cap** clamping both; a **depth-adjusting nut** and **lateral adjusting lever** behind; a **handle** at the rear and a **knob** at the front.

topics.why: Softwood vs hardwood, seasoning and the defects of timber (knots, shakes, warping) are the most-asked theory questions of the carpentry unit.
topics.gist:
**Structure of a tree trunk** (cross-section, outside in): bark, **cambium** (growing layer), **sapwood** (light, living, carries sap, weaker), **heartwood** (dark, dead, strong, durable), **pith** at the centre, **annual rings** (one per year) and **medullary rays** running radially.

**Softwood** comes from **conifers** (needle leaves, evergreen): light colour, light weight, resinous, distinct annual rings, non-porous, easy to work, less durable. Examples: **deodar** (furniture, doors, sleepers), **chir/pine** (packing cases, cheap furniture, patterns), fir, spruce, kail.

**Hardwood** comes from **deciduous, broad-leaved** trees: darker, heavier, porous (vessels), closer grain, stronger and more durable, harder to work. Examples: **teak** (best Indian timber: furniture, doors, windows, ship building, patterns), **sal** (beams, railway sleepers, heavy construction), **sheesham** (furniture, cabinets, carving), **mango** (packing boxes, cheap furniture), **babul** (cart wheels, agricultural implements, tool handles), oak, mahogany, walnut.

**Seasoning** removes moisture (green timber can be 50% or more) down to about **10-15%** (8-12% for furniture), so the wood does not shrink, warp, crack or rot. **Natural (air) seasoning** is slow but cheap; **artificial** methods (kiln, water, boiling, chemical, electrical) are fast and controlled.

**Defects:** natural (**knots**, **shakes**: heart, star, cup/ring, radial; twisted fibres, upsets, rind galls), seasoning defects (**warp**: bow, cup, twist; **checks**, splits, honeycombing, case hardening), fungi and insects (dry rot, wet rot, termites), conversion defects (wane, torn grain, diagonal grain). **Manufactured wood:** plywood, block board, particle board, hardboard.

Manufactured boards: plywood (odd number of veneers, grain crossed), particle board, hardboard

Putting teak under softwood or deodar under hardwood

questions.q: What is seasoning of timber? Explain its methods and objectives.
questions.a:
**Seasoning** is the controlled removal of moisture (sap) from freshly cut (green) timber down to about 10-15% (8-12% for furniture), close to the moisture it will have in service.

**Objectives:** reduce weight; increase strength, hardness and durability; prevent shrinkage, warping and cracking in service; make it resistant to fungi and insects; improve workability, gluing and painting.

**Methods:**
1. **Natural / air seasoning**: planks stacked under a shed with spacers so air circulates; cheap but slow (months to years), uneven.
2. **Water seasoning**: logs immersed in running water to wash out sap, then air-dried.
3. **Boiling / steaming**: quick, reduces sap, but costly.
4. **Kiln seasoning**: in a chamber with controlled hot air, humidity and circulation; fast (days), uniform, the industrial method.
5. **Chemical seasoning**: salt solutions (urea, NaCl) slow surface drying to avoid cracking.
6. **Electrical seasoning**: high-frequency current heats the wood throughout.

questions.q: A timber sample weighs 5.0 kg when cut and 4.2 kg after oven drying. Find its moisture content and say whether it is fit for furniture.
questions.a:
$$MC = \frac{5.0 - 4.2}{4.2} \times 100 = \frac{0.8}{4.2} \times 100 = 19.05\%$$
Furniture timber should be about 8-12% (at most ~15%), so this timber is **not adequately seasoned**; it would shrink and warp in service.

questions.q: Explain any four defects in timber.
questions.a:
1. **Knots**: dark, hard spots where a branch grew from the trunk; break the continuity of fibres and weaken the timber; dead (loose) knots may fall out.
2. **Shakes**: cracks separating fibres. *Heart shake*: radial cracks from the pith; *star shake*: from the bark inwards; *cup/ring shake*: along an annual ring; caused by shrinkage or wind stresses.
3. **Warping**: distortion during seasoning due to uneven shrinkage: *bow* (along length), *cup* (across width), *twist* (spiral).
4. **Checks and splits**: cracks across or along the grain at the surface or ends from too-rapid drying.
5. **Dry rot / wet rot**: fungal decay that turns wood to powder; **termites** eat the interior.
6. **Upsets**: fibres crushed by wrong felling. (Any four, with a short sketch description of each.)

topics.why: Rarely more than a 2-3 mark 'name the fastening devices' question, but it fills a short answer and viva easily.
topics.gist:
**Carpentry hardware** means the metal fittings and fastenings used to join, hinge, lock and finish wooden work.

**Nails** (mild steel wire, sometimes galvanised or brass): wire nails (round head), oval nails, cut nails, clout nails (large flat head for roofing felt), lost-head/panel pins (head punched below the surface), and brads. Specified by **length**, and by **gauge** (wire diameter). Driven slightly inclined (dovetail nailing) for better grip, kept away from ends to avoid splitting.

**Wood screws** hold better than nails and can be removed: **countersunk** (flat head, finishes flush), **round head**, **raised (oval) head**; slotted or Phillips/cross drive. Specified by **length and gauge number**. A **pilot hole** is drilled first, a clearance hole in the top piece, and the hole countersunk.

**Bolts and coach screws**: carriage bolt (round head, square neck that bites into the wood), coach screw (square head, driven with a spanner) for heavy work.

**Hinges:** **butt hinge** (doors, windows), **T-hinge** and **strap hinge** (gates, heavy doors), **piano (continuous) hinge** (box lids), **parliament hinge** (doors that must swing clear of the wall), spring hinges.

**Others:** tower bolts, latches, locks, handles, hasp and staple, brackets, angle plates, corrugated fasteners (for butt joints), wooden **dowels** and **adhesives**: animal (hide) glue, casein, PVA (white glue), urea-formaldehyde and epoxy resins.
