questions.q: Why is a pilot hole drilled before driving a wood screw?
questions.a: The pilot hole (smaller than the root diameter of the screw) guides the screw straight, prevents the wood (especially hardwood or near edges) from splitting, reduces the driving torque and avoids breaking the screw, while leaving enough wood for the thread to grip. A clearance hole is drilled in the top piece so it is pulled tight against the lower one.

topics.why: The operations and especially the wood joints (lap, mortise and tenon, dovetail, bridle) are sketched in exams, and the shop job is one of these joints, so the viva centres here.
topics.gist:
**Basic carpentry operations:**
- **Marking and measuring**: from a face side and face edge (marked with face marks), using try square, marking gauge, mortise gauge.
- **Sawing**: ripping (along the grain), cross-cutting (across), cutting tenons and shoulders with a tenon saw; saw on the waste side of the line.
- **Planing**: face side first, then face edge square to it, then width and thickness to the gauge lines; plane with the grain.
- **Chiselling**: paring (removing thin slices by hand pressure), chopping (mortising with mallet), grooving and housing.
- **Boring** with brace and bit or drill; **rebating**, **grooving**, **chamfering**, **moulding** and **sanding / finishing**.

**Wood joints** (know a sketch for each):
- **Lap (halving) joints**: cross-lap, T-lap (tee halving), corner lap; half the thickness removed from each piece so faces are flush. Frames, the usual first shop job.
- **Mortise and tenon**: a rectangular projection (tenon, about one-third of the thickness) fits into a matching hole (mortise); strong, used in doors, windows, tables, chairs.
- **Bridle joint**: an open mortise (slot) at the end of one piece receives a tenon-like piece; frames and legs.
- **Dovetail joint**: flared tails interlock with pins and resist pulling apart; drawers and boxes. Slope about 1:6 for softwood, 1:8 for hardwood.
- **Butt, mitre (45°), dowel, tongue and groove, housing (dado), dovetail-lap** joints.

questions.q: Sketch any four wood joints and state their applications.
questions.a:
1. **Cross-lap joint**: two pieces crossing at 90°, each cut to half depth for the width of the other, faces flush. Use: frames, partitions, stands.
2. **T-lap joint**: one piece's end halved into the middle of the other, forming a T. Use: frames, rails meeting stiles.
3. **Mortise and tenon joint**: a tenon (about T/3 thick) on one member fits into a rectangular mortise in the other; may be through or stub, often wedged or pinned. Use: doors, windows, tables, chairs.
4. **Dovetail joint**: fan-shaped tails on one board interlock with pins on the other (slope 1:6 to 1:8). Use: drawers, boxes, cabinets.
5. **Bridle joint**: an open slot in one member receives the other. Use: frames, leg-and-rail joints.
6. **Mitre joint**: ends cut at 45° to form a 90° corner. Use: picture frames.
(Any four, each with a clear sketch description.)

questions.q: Write the sequence of operations for making a T-lap joint.
questions.a:
1. Check the stock; plane the face side and face edge, mark face marks.
2. Plane to width and thickness using the marking gauge.
3. Cut both pieces to length (crosscut saw), square the ends.
4. On the cross piece, mark the width of the stem piece with try square and knife; on the stem, mark the shoulder at the width of the cross piece.
5. Gauge half the thickness on both pieces from the face side.
6. Saw the shoulders down to the gauge line with the tenon saw (in the waste).
7. Saw the cheek of the stem piece along the grain; on the cross piece make several saw cuts in the waste.
8. Remove waste with firmer chisel and mallet; pare the bottom flat to the line.
9. Trial-fit, correct high spots, check squareness with a try square.
10. Finish with smoothing plane and sandpaper.

questions.q: Why are a face side and a face edge prepared first in carpentry?
questions.a: They are the reference (datum) surfaces: planed straight, flat and square to each other, they let all other markings (width, thickness, shoulders, mortises) be gauged and squared from a true surface, so that every piece and joint ends up consistent and square. Face marks are pencilled on them so they are not confused later.

topics.why: Seldom more than a 2-3 mark list in the theory paper, but almost always asked in the practical viva and expected in the records.
topics.gist:
Wood shop accidents come from sharp edges, flying chips, tools slipping and, on machines, rotating cutters. A good answer is organised by **personal**, **tool**, **work** and **machine** safety.

**Personal:** wear an apron/close-fitting clothes, no loose sleeves, ties or jewellery, tie long hair; safety shoes; goggles when chiselling, sanding or on machines; dust mask while sanding; no fooling around in the shop.

**Hand tools:** keep tools sharp (a blunt tool needs force and slips), use the right tool for the job, never use a chisel or file without a handle, and keep both hands **behind the cutting edge**, cutting away from the body. Strike chisels with a mallet. Lay planes on their side (or with the blade retracted) so the edge is not damaged. Carry sharp tools pointing down; never keep chisels or saws in pockets. Return tools to the rack.

**Work holding:** clamp the work in the vice or with a bench hook/G-clamp before sawing or chiselling; check the wood for nails before planing or sawing.

**Machines (circular saw, band saw, planer, lathe):** use guards, push sticks for short pieces, never adjust while running, switch off and wait for the cutter to stop, one operator only, and know the emergency stop.

**Shop:** keep the floor clean of shavings (slips, fire), no smoking or open flames near wood dust and finishes, fire extinguisher and first-aid box within reach, report every injury.

questions.q: Why is a sharp tool safer than a blunt one?
questions.a: A sharp tool cuts with little force, so it stays under control. A blunt tool needs extra force, tends to skid or jump off the work and can slip suddenly into the hand or body; it also tears the wood, needing even more force.

questions.q: Why must timber be checked for nails before planing or sawing?
questions.a: A hidden nail chips or breaks the plane iron and saw teeth, and the tool can jerk or fragments can fly, injuring the worker. Removing nails (or marking them) protects both the tool and the user.

topics.why: 'Name and sketch hand moulding tools' (riddle, rammer, sprue pin, vent wire, lifter, slick, strike-off bar) is a regular 5-mark question and the viva starts here.
topics.gist:
Its tools fall into hand tools, flasks and melting/pouring equipment.

**Hand moulding tools:**
- **Shovel**: mixing and moving sand. **Riddle**: a sieve (wire mesh in a wooden frame) to remove lumps and foreign matter, used to riddle facing sand over the pattern.
- **Rammers**: **peen** (wedge-shaped) end for ramming in corners and close to the pattern, **butt** (flat) end for finishing the top.
- **Strike-off bar**: a straight bar that levels the sand flush with the top of the flask.
- **Sprue pin** (and riser pin): tapered wooden pin forming the sprue (down-gate) and riser.
- **Vent wire / vent rod**: makes vent holes so gases and steam escape.
- **Draw spike / draw screw** and **rapping plate**: rap (loosen) and lift the pattern.
- **Lifter**: lifts loose sand from deep narrow pockets and finishes the bottom.
- **Trowels and slicks**: finish and repair flat and curved surfaces; **gate cutter**: cuts the runner and ingates.
- **Swab**: moistens the sand edges around the pattern before withdrawal. **Bellows**: blows loose sand out of the cavity. **Gaggers**: iron pieces that reinforce hanging sand in the cope.

**Flasks (moulding boxes):** wooden or metal frames, the top one the **cope**, the bottom one the **drag**, any intermediate one the **cheek**, aligned by pins and lugs. **Moulding board** supports the pattern and drag.

**Melting and pouring:** **cupola** (cast iron), crucible/pit furnace (non-ferrous), electric furnaces; **ladles** (hand shank, bull ladle, crane ladle), crucibles, tongs, skimmer.

questions.q: Sketch and describe any five hand moulding tools used in the foundry.
questions.a:
1. **Riddle**: a round or square wooden frame with a wire mesh bottom; sieves sand to remove lumps and foreign matter.
2. **Rammer**: a wooden or metal tool with a wedge-shaped **peen end** (rams sand near the pattern and in corners) and a flat **butt end** (finishes the top).
3. **Strike-off bar**: a straight-edged wooden or steel bar that scrapes excess sand level with the flask top.
4. **Sprue pin**: a tapered round wooden pin placed in the cope before ramming and withdrawn to leave the sprue.
5. **Vent wire**: a thin steel wire with a pointed end and a loop handle; pierces vents in the rammed sand.
6. **Draw spike**: a pointed steel rod with an eye; driven into the pattern to rap and lift it.
7. **Trowel / slick**: flat steel blades with handles to smooth and repair the mould surfaces.
8. **Lifter**: thin bent steel strip for deep pockets.
(Any five, each with a short sketch description.)

questions.q: What are cope, drag and cheek?
questions.a: They are the parts of a moulding flask (box). The **drag** is the lower box, rammed first with the pattern on the moulding board; the **cope** is the upper box placed on the drag and carrying the sprue and riser; a **cheek** is an intermediate box used between them for a three-part mould of tall or complex patterns. They are aligned by pins and lugs and clamped before pouring.

questions.q: Why should the rammer's peen end be used near the pattern and the butt end at the top?
questions.a: The narrow peen end concentrates the force, packing sand firmly into corners and around the pattern, which gives a hard, accurate mould face. The flat butt end compacts the top layers evenly and finishes the surface before striking off. Using the flat end near the pattern leaves soft sand there (swells, metal penetration).

topics.why: Definition, pattern materials with merits, pattern vs casting differences and the colour code are common 3-5 mark questions; the pattern-to-casting weight ratio is an occasional numerical.
topics.gist:
A **pattern** is a **replica of the object to be cast**, used to make the mould cavity. It is **not identical** to the casting: it is made larger by the **allowances** (shrinkage, machining, draft...), it carries **core prints** to seat cores, may be split for withdrawal, and holes are not shown where a core forms them.

**Pattern materials:**
- **Wood** (teak, pine, deodar, mahogany): cheap, light, easy to shape and repair; but absorbs moisture, warps, wears. For small numbers of castings.
- **Metal** (aluminium, cast iron, brass, steel, white metal): accurate, durable, smooth, does not warp; costly and heavier. For mass production and machine moulding (match plates).
- **Plastics / epoxy resins**: light, smooth, strong, moisture-proof.
- **Plaster of Paris**: easily shaped, intricate detail, used for small patterns and core boxes.
- **Wax** (investment casting) and **expanded polystyrene** (full mould / lost foam), which are not withdrawn but melted or vaporised.

**Factors in selecting the material:** number of castings, size and complexity, accuracy and finish required, moulding method (hand/machine), casting process, cost.

**Colour code** (a common Indian/US convention; manuals vary): surfaces left **unmachined: black**; surfaces to be **machined: red**; **core prints: yellow**; seats of **loose pieces: red stripes on yellow**; **stop-offs: black diagonal stripes on yellow**. Wood patterns are varnished or shellacked to seal moisture.

**Core prints** are projections on the pattern that leave recesses (seats) in the mould to locate and support the core.

Pattern ≠ casting: allowances, core prints, split/loose pieces, cored holes omitted, different material

questions.q: State the differences between a pattern and the casting made from it.
questions.a:
1. **Size:** pattern is larger by the shrinkage, machining and other allowances.
2. **Core prints:** pattern carries core prints; the casting does not.
3. **Holes:** cored holes and cavities are not on the pattern (they come from cores).
4. **Construction:** pattern may be split into parts or have loose pieces; casting is one piece.
5. **Draft:** pattern's vertical faces are tapered; casting may need these machined off.
6. **Material:** pattern is usually wood/metal/plastic; the casting is the cast metal.
7. **Finish/colour:** pattern is painted to the colour code.

questions.q: Discuss wood and metal as pattern materials with their merits and demerits.
questions.a:
**Wood (teak, pine, deodar, mahogany):**
- Merits: cheap, light, easily shaped, joined and repaired; readily available; good for small runs and large patterns.
- Demerits: absorbs moisture and warps, swells or shrinks; wears and loses accuracy quickly; short life.

**Metal (aluminium, cast iron, brass, steel, white metal):**
- Merits: accurate and dimensionally stable; long life; smooth surface for good casting finish; does not absorb moisture; suitable for machine moulding and match plates.
- Demerits: expensive; heavy (except Al); needs machining to make; difficult to repair or modify; cast iron rusts.

**Choice:** wood for few castings, metal for mass production.

questions.q: A pine pattern weighs 1.5 kg. Estimate the weight of the cast iron casting made from it. (Density of pine 0.5 g/cc, cast iron 7.2 g/cc.)
questions.a:
$$W_c \approx W_p \frac{\rho_{CI}}{\rho_{pine}} = 1.5 \times \frac{7.2}{0.5} = 1.5 \times 14.4 = 21.6\ \text{kg}$$
The real casting is slightly lighter, because the pattern is oversize by the allowances (and cored holes reduce it further).

questions.q: State the colour code used on patterns.
questions.a:
(Common Indian/American convention; check the shop manual.)
- Surfaces to be left unmachined (as cast): **black**
- Surfaces to be machined: **red**
- Core prints and seats for cores: **yellow**
- Seats of loose pieces: **red stripes on a yellow background**
- Stop-offs (pieces to be filled with sand): **black diagonal stripes on yellow**
Purpose: the moulder knows at a glance which surfaces have machining allowance, where cores go and which pieces are loose.

topics.why: 'Explain different types of patterns with neat sketches' is perhaps the most predictable 5-8 mark question of the foundry unit.
topics.gist:
1. **Solid (single-piece) pattern**: one piece, no joints; for simple shapes with one flat side (e.g. a stuffing box, a block). Cheapest; few castings.
2. **Split (two-piece / multi-piece) pattern**: split along the parting line into halves aligned by **dowel pins**; one half moulded in the drag, the other in the cope. For complex shapes that cannot be withdrawn in one piece (pipes, spindles, cylinders, taps).
3. **Loose-piece pattern**: projections (bosses) that would prevent withdrawal are attached by **wooden pins** and drawn out sideways after the main body.
4. **Match-plate pattern**: cope and drag halves mounted on opposite sides of a metal (aluminium) plate, often with gates and runners. For **mass production of small castings** on moulding machines; accurate but costly.
5. **Cope and drag pattern**: halves mounted on separate plates rammed separately, for large heavy castings.
6. **Gated pattern**: several patterns joined by gates and runners for multiple small castings in one mould.
7. **Sweep pattern**: a board shaped to the profile, rotated about a spindle to sweep out the mould; for large **axisymmetric** castings (bells, large pulleys, kettles).
8. **Skeleton pattern**: a wooden framework (ribs) filled with loam and strickled; for large castings in small numbers (water pipes, turbine casings, large bends).
9. **Segmental pattern**: a segment rotated about a centre to form a circular mould (large gears, rings).
10. **Follow-board pattern**: a board shaped to support a weak or thin pattern during ramming.

questions.q: Explain the different types of patterns with sketches and applications.
questions.a:
1. **Single-piece (solid)**: one solid piece (sketch: a plain block on the moulding board). Simple castings, few numbers, e.g. a gland, a block.
2. **Split**: two halves joined at the parting line with dowel pins (sketch: a cylinder split lengthwise, pins in one half). Pipes, cylinders, spindles.
3. **Loose-piece**: main body with bosses fixed by pins (sketch: a block with a side boss held by a wooden pin). Castings with projections that would obstruct withdrawal.
4. **Match plate**: half pattern on each side of a plate with runner and gates (sketch: plate with bosses on both faces). Mass production of small castings.
5. **Cope and drag**: halves on separate plates. Large, heavy castings rammed separately.
6. **Gated**: several small patterns joined by gates. Many small castings per mould.
7. **Sweep**: profile board on a spindle (sketch: vertical spindle with an arm carrying the profile). Bells, large pulleys.
8. **Skeleton**: ribbed framework (sketch: open wooden ribs of a pipe bend). Large castings in small numbers.
9. **Segmental**: a segment indexed round a pivot. Large rings, gear blanks.
10. **Follow board**: a board shaped to fit and support a weak pattern while ramming.

questions.q: What is a loose-piece pattern? How is it withdrawn from the mould?
questions.a: A loose-piece pattern has projections (bosses, ribs) that are not fixed to the main body but held by loose wooden pins or dovetails, because if fixed they would tear the sand when the pattern is drawn. Ramming firmly around the loose piece, the pins are pulled out; the main pattern is withdrawn first, and then the loose pieces are drawn sideways into the cavity and lifted out. The moulder needs skill, and the pieces must not be lost.

questions.q: Compare a sweep pattern and a skeleton pattern.
questions.a: **Sweep:** a profile board mounted on a vertical spindle and rotated to sweep out a mould; only for castings symmetric about an axis (bells, kettles, large pulleys). **Skeleton:** an open wooden framework of the outline, the spaces filled with loam and strickled; for large castings of any regular shape (pipe bends, turbine casings, valve bodies) required in small numbers. Both save pattern material and cost for large castings; both demand skilled moulders.

topics.why: The guaranteed foundry question: list and explain the allowances with typical values, and a numerical giving pattern dimensions from casting dimensions.
topics.gist:
The pattern is made bigger (once, smaller) than the casting so the casting finishes at drawing size:

1. **Shrinkage (contraction) allowance**: metal contracts in three stages: liquid contraction, solidification shrinkage and **solid contraction** from the freezing point to room temperature. The first two are made up by the **riser**; the **pattern allowance covers only solid contraction**. It is given in **mm per metre** (built in with a **shrink rule**). Typical values (vary by text): **grey cast iron about 10 mm/m (7-10.5)**, **steel about 20 mm/m (16-21)**, **aluminium about 13 mm/m (13-17)**, **brass about 15 mm/m**.
2. **Machining (finish) allowance**: extra metal on surfaces to be machined, because cast surfaces are rough, scaled or decarburised. Roughly **2-6 mm for cast iron**, more for steel (scale), less (1.5-3 mm) for non-ferrous. Added on each machined face; for **holes it is subtracted** (the cast hole is smaller and is machined out).
3. **Draft (taper) allowance**: a taper on faces parallel to the direction of withdrawal so the pattern lifts without tearing the sand. About **1-3°** on external surfaces, **more on internal surfaces** (the sand inside grips the pattern).
4. **Distortion (camber) allowance**: long flat plates and U/V-shaped castings warp on cooling as the thin and thick parts contract unevenly; the pattern is bent **in the opposite direction** by the expected amount.
5. **Shake (rapping) allowance**: rapping the pattern to free it **enlarges the cavity**, so the pattern is made slightly **smaller**. It is the only **negative** allowance.
key_points: Five allowances: shrinkage, machining, draft, distortion, shake
Shrinkage allowance covers solid contraction only; liquid and solidification shrinkage are fed by the riser
Typical shrinkage: grey CI ~10 mm/m, steel ~20 mm/m, Al ~13 mm/m, brass ~15 mm/m
Shrink rule: graduated longer by the shrinkage, read directly
Machining allowance added to external machined faces, subtracted from holes; CI ~2-6 mm, steel more, non-ferrous less
Draft: 1-3° external, more on internal faces; on surfaces parallel to withdrawal
Distortion: pattern bent opposite to expected warping
Shake: negative allowance, pattern made smaller
Order: add machining to the finished size first, then apply shrinkage to that
formulas: $L_p = L_c\,(1 + s)$ — pattern length for casting length $L_c$, shrinkage $s$ (e.g. $s = 10/1000$ for 10 mm/m)
$L_p = (L_f + 2m)(1 + s)$ — external dimension machined both sides, allowance $m$ per side
$D_p = (D_f - 2m)(1 + s)$ — hole/core diameter machined to $D_f$
$x = h \tan\theta$ — draft offset on a face of height $h$ for draft angle $\theta$
traps: Saying shrinkage allowance compensates all three contractions; the riser feeds liquid and solidification shrinkage
Adding machining allowance to a hole diameter; it is subtracted
Applying shrinkage before machining allowance; apply it to (finished size + machining)
Calling machining allowance negative; only shake allowance is negative
Typical values differ between books; quote a range and say 'typical'
Draft on internal surfaces is larger, not smaller

options: Solid contraction from freezing to room temperature
questions.a: Solid-state contraction is allowed on the pattern; liquid and solidification shrinkage are fed by risers.

questions.q: The typical shrinkage allowance for grey cast iron is about

questions.q: Explain the various allowances provided on a pattern, with typical values.
questions.a:
1. **Shrinkage allowance**: compensates for solid contraction of the casting from the freezing point to room temperature (riser feeds liquid and solidification shrinkage). Given in mm/m and built in with a shrink rule. Typical: grey CI 7-10.5 (≈10) mm/m, steel 16-21 (≈20), aluminium ≈13, brass ≈15, white CI ≈21.
2. **Machining allowance**: extra metal on surfaces to be machined, to remove scale, sand, roughness and decarburised skin. Depends on metal, size, method and position (cope surfaces get more): CI ≈2-6 mm, steel ≈3-10 mm, non-ferrous ≈1.5-3 mm. Added to outside faces, subtracted from holes.
3. **Draft allowance**: taper on faces parallel to the direction of withdrawal so the pattern lifts without damaging the mould. External ≈1-2° (or 10-25 mm/m), internal ≈2-3° (larger because sand inside grips), less on metal patterns.
4. **Distortion (camber) allowance**: for long, flat, U or V shapes that warp on cooling; the pattern is distorted equally in the opposite direction.
5. **Shake (rapping) allowance**: negative; rapping enlarges the cavity, so the pattern is made slightly smaller (≈0.5-1 mm on large patterns, often neglected on small ones).

questions.q: A grey cast iron block of finished size 200 × 100 × 50 mm is to be machined on all faces. Machining allowance is 3 mm per face and shrinkage allowance 10 mm/m. Find the pattern dimensions (neglect draft and shake).
questions.a:
Add machining to each face, then apply shrinkage ($s = 0.01$):

Length: $(200 + 2\times3)(1.01) = 206 \times 1.01 = 208.06$ mm

Width: $(100 + 6)(1.01) = 106 \times 1.01 = 107.06$ mm

Thickness: $(50 + 6)(1.01) = 56 \times 1.01 = 56.56$ mm

**Pattern: 208.06 × 107.06 × 56.56 mm.**

questions.q: A cast iron flange has finished outside diameter 200 mm, bore 80 mm and thickness 30 mm, all machined. Machining allowance is 3 mm per surface, shrinkage 10 mm/m, draft 1° on the outer vertical face. Find the pattern OD, core (bore) diameter and thickness, and the draft offset.
questions.a:
$s = 0.01$, $m = 3$ mm.

**OD** (external, add): $(200 + 6)(1.01) = 208.06$ mm

**Bore** (internal, subtract machining): $(80 - 6)(1.01) = 74 \times 1.01 = 74.74$ mm (core / core print diameter)

**Thickness**: $(30 + 6)(1.01) = 36.36$ mm

**Draft** on the outer face of height 36.36 mm:
$$x = h\tan 1^\circ = 36.36 \times 0.01746 = 0.63\ \text{mm}$$
Draft is added as extra material: the OD is 208.06 mm at the face farthest from the parting line and grows by 0.63 mm per side towards the parting face, i.e. about $208.06 + 2 \times 0.63 = 209.33$ mm there, so the pattern draws out of the sand without tearing it.

questions.q: A steel bar casting is to be 500 mm long. The shrinkage allowance for steel is 20 mm/m. What length should the pattern be, and what is a shrink rule?
questions.a:
$$L_p = 500(1 + 0.020) = 500 \times 1.02 = 510\ \text{mm}$$
A **shrink rule** is a pattern maker's rule whose graduations are longer than standard by the shrinkage allowance of a given metal (e.g. a 1 m 'steel' rule actually measures 1.02 m). The pattern maker reads the casting dimension directly from it and the shrinkage is built in automatically.

questions.q: Why is draft allowance larger on internal surfaces than on external surfaces?
questions.a: When the pattern is withdrawn, an internal surface (e.g. a pocket or the inside of a hollow pattern) has sand on all sides that is compressed against it and also tends to close in as the pattern lifts, so it grips the pattern more and is easily torn. External surfaces have sand on one side only and the sand can move away slightly. A larger taper inside (≈2-3° vs ≈1°) lets the pattern clear the sand without damage.

topics.why: Properties of moulding sand and the composition of green sand are asked in nearly every paper; types of sand and the permeability test add short answers and a small numerical.
topics.gist:
Moulding sand forms the mould cavity, so it must hold shape, let gases out, survive molten metal and then break away from the casting.

**Composition of green (moulding) sand** (typical; ranges vary by text):
- **Silica sand (SiO₂)** about 75-85%: the refractory grains.
- **Clay (binder)** about 10-15% (bentonite or fireclay): gives strength and plasticity.
- **Water** about 2-8% (commonly 4-6%): activates the clay.
- **Additives** a few %: sea coal (finish), cereal/dextrin (strength), wood flour/sawdust (collapsibility).

**Properties:**
1. **Porosity / permeability**: lets steam and gases escape (else blowholes).
2. **Plasticity / flowability**: flows around the pattern and takes its shape when rammed.
3. **Adhesiveness**: sticks to the flask walls.
4. **Cohesiveness / strength**: green strength, dry strength, hot strength, so the mould does not collapse or erode.
5. **Refractoriness**: withstands the pouring temperature without fusing.
6. **Collapsibility**: breaks down after solidification so the casting can contract freely (else hot tears) and be knocked out.
7. **Durability / reusability**, fine grain for finish, chemical inertness, thermal stability, low cost.

**Types:** **green sand** (moist, the common one), **dry sand** (green sand baked, stronger, for large castings), **loam sand** (about 50% clay, for large castings with sweep/skeleton patterns), **facing sand** (fresh, fine, next to the pattern), **backing / floor sand** (used sand that fills the rest of the box), **system sand** (for machine moulding), **parting sand** (clay-free dry silica sprinkled to stop cope and drag sticking), **core sand** (sand + oil binder).

questions.q: Explain the properties of good moulding sand.
questions.a:
1. **Permeability (porosity)**: allows steam and gases from the metal and mould to escape; low permeability causes blowholes and gas porosity.
2. **Plasticity / flowability**: sand flows and packs uniformly around the pattern under ramming and retains the shape.
3. **Adhesiveness**: sticks to the flask walls so the sand mass does not fall out when the cope is lifted.
4. **Cohesiveness (strength)**: grains hold together: green strength (handling), dry strength (resists erosion and metal pressure), hot strength (does not crack at high temperature).
5. **Refractoriness**: withstands the pouring temperature without fusing on to the casting.
6. **Collapsibility**: breaks down after solidification, allowing contraction and easy knock-out; prevents hot tears.
7. **Durability / reusability**: can be reconditioned and reused many times.
8. **Fineness**: fine grains give good surface finish (but lower permeability, a trade-off).
9. **Chemical inertness, thermal stability, low cost and availability.**

- Water: $0.05 \times 50 = 2.5$ kg

questions.a: **Facing sand:** fresh, fine-grained sand (new silica, clay and additives like coal dust) riddled directly over the pattern in a layer 20-30 mm thick; it forms the mould face that touches the metal, so it needs high strength and refractoriness and gives a good finish. **Backing (floor) sand:** used, reconditioned sand (often black from burnt coal dust) that fills the rest of the flask behind the facing sand; cheaper, lower properties, mainly supports the facing.

topics.why: Classification questions (green/dry/skin-dried/loam/CO₂/metallic; bench/floor/pit/machine) appear for 3-5 marks; green vs dry sand mould is a common comparison.
topics.gist:
Moulds are classified two ways.

**By mould material:**
- **Green sand mould**: moist sand, poured without drying. Cheapest and quickest; used for most small and medium ferrous and non-ferrous castings. Limits: low strength, moisture can cause blowholes, not for very large or intricate castings.
- **Dry sand mould**: green sand mould baked in an oven (about 150-350 °C) to drive out moisture; stronger, more permeable, better finish and accuracy; used for large castings; costlier and slower.
- **Skin-dried mould**: only the face (15-25 mm) is dried by a torch or heater; a compromise for large moulds.
- **Loam mould**: loam (about 50% clay) built up on brick and iron frameworks with sweep or skeleton patterns, dried; for very large castings (bells, cylinders).
- **CO₂ mould**: sand with 3-6% sodium silicate hardened by CO₂ gas; strong, accurate, quick.
- **Shell, investment, plaster, cement-bonded** moulds.
- **Metallic (permanent) moulds**: cast iron or steel dies reused for thousands of castings (gravity die casting, pressure die casting) of non-ferrous metals.

**By method / where moulded:**
- **Bench moulding**: small flasks on a bench.
- **Floor moulding**: medium/large moulds on the foundry floor, floor acting as drag.
- **Pit moulding**: very large castings in a pit in the floor, with the pit as drag.
- **Machine moulding**: moulding machines (jolt, squeeze, jolt-squeeze, sand slinger) for mass production.

Moulds are also **expendable** (sand, shell, investment: destroyed to remove the casting) or **permanent** (metal).

questions.q: Classify moulds with a brief description of each.
questions.a:
**A. According to mould material:**
1. Green sand mould: moist sand, not dried; common for small/medium castings.
2. Dry sand mould: baked green sand mould; large castings.
3. Skin-dried mould: only the face dried.
4. Loam mould: high-clay loam on brick/iron framework; very large castings.
5. CO₂ mould: sodium silicate sand hardened by CO₂.
6. Shell, investment, plaster moulds: precision castings.
7. Metallic (permanent) mould: reusable metal dies for non-ferrous castings.

**B. According to method:**
1. Bench moulding: small flasks on a bench.
2. Floor moulding: on the foundry floor.
3. Pit moulding: in a pit, for very large castings.
4. Machine moulding: jolt, squeeze, sand slinger; mass production.

questions.q: What are the advantages and limitations of green sand moulds?
questions.a:
**Advantages:** cheapest and quickest; no baking; sand can be reused after reconditioning; collapsible, so fewer hot tears; suitable for most ferrous and non-ferrous metals and for machine moulding.

**Limitations:** low strength, so not for very large or heavy castings; moisture can generate steam and cause blowholes, scabs and pinholes; poorer dimensional accuracy and finish than dry, shell or investment moulds; mould must be poured soon after making.

topics.why: 'Explain the procedure for making a green sand mould with a split pattern, with neat sketches' is a classic 5-8 mark question and it is exactly what the practical exam asks you to do.
topics.gist:
The standard shop exercise is a **two-box green sand mould with a split pattern**.

**Drag:** (1) put the drag half of the pattern flat face down on the **moulding board** with the drag box upside down around it; (2) sprinkle **parting sand** and riddle 20-30 mm of **facing sand** over the pattern; (3) fill **backing sand** in layers and **ram**, peen end near the pattern, butt end on top (too soft gives swells, too hard gives blowholes); (4) **strike off** and **vent**; (5) **roll the drag over**.

**Cope:** (6) remove the board, place the **cope half** of the pattern on the dowels and sprinkle parting sand; (7) put the cope box on and set the **sprue pin** and **riser pin**; (8) riddle, fill, ram, strike off, vent; (9) pull the pins and cut a **pouring basin**.

**Finishing:** (10) lift the cope, **swab** the edges, **rap** and **draw** both pattern halves; (11) cut the **runner and ingate** with a gate cutter, repair with lifter, trowel and slick, blow out loose sand; (12) set any **core** in its prints; (13) **close** the mould on its pins, weight or clamp the cope against the metal's lifting force, and **pour**.

**Gating system:** pouring basin → tapered sprue → sprue well → runner → ingate → cavity, plus a **riser** that feeds shrinkage and shows the mould is full.

1. Place the drag half of the pattern flat on the moulding board; invert the drag box around it.
2. Sprinkle parting sand; riddle 20-30 mm of facing sand over the pattern.
3. Fill backing sand in layers, ramming with the peen end near the pattern, the butt end at the top.

5. Roll the drag over on a bottom board; remove the moulding board; smooth the parting surface.

10. Lift off the cope; swab around the pattern; rap and withdraw both pattern halves with a draw spike.
11. Cut runner and ingates with a gate cutter; repair with trowel, slick and lifter; blow out loose sand.
12. Place the core (if any) in the core prints.
13. Close the mould, clamp or weight the cope, and pour.

**Sketch description of the closed mould (section):** drag box below, cope box above, meeting at the parting line; the mould cavity of the casting shape across the parting line; a pouring basin on top of the cope leading into a tapered sprue down to the parting level, a sprue well at its base, a runner along the parting surface and an ingate into the cavity; a riser rising from the cavity through the cope; vent holes above the cavity; a core resting in core-print seats across the cavity; weights on the cope.

questions.q: Name the elements of a gating system and state the function of each.
questions.a:
1. **Pouring basin (cup)**: receives the metal from the ladle and reduces turbulence; holds back slag.
2. **Sprue (down-gate)**: tapered vertical channel carrying metal to the parting level; taper prevents air aspiration.
3. **Sprue well (base)**: cushions the falling stream, reduces erosion and turbulence.
4. **Runner**: horizontal channel distributing metal to the ingates; traps slag.
5. **Ingate (gate)**: admits metal into the cavity.
6. **Riser**: reservoir feeding shrinkage, shows mould is full, lets gases out.
(Also: skim bob, choke, strainer core for slag control.)

questions.q: Why are weights placed on the cope before pouring? Estimate the lifting force for a cavity of parting area 0.04 m² with 0.15 m of cast iron (7000 kg/m³) above it.
questions.a:
Molten metal exerts metallostatic pressure upward on the cope over the parting area; if this exceeds the cope's weight, the cope lifts and metal runs out at the parting line (run-out, fins).
$$F = \rho g h A = 7000 \times 9.81 \times 0.15 \times 0.04 = 412\ \text{N} \approx 42\ \text{kgf}$$
So the cope plus weights must exceed about 42 kg (with a safety factor, and extra for any cores pushed upward by buoyancy).

questions.q: Why is the drag rolled over during moulding?
questions.a: The drag is rammed upside down with the pattern's flat face on the moulding board so that sand can be packed firmly over the pattern. Rolling it over brings the flat pattern face and the parting surface to the top, ready for the cope half of the pattern and the cope box to be placed on it; the drag's open bottom then rests on a bottom board.

topics.why: Short notes on CO₂, shell and investment moulding and machine moulding appear, and the casting-defects question (causes and remedies), usually asked with this unit, is a reliable 5-8 marker.
topics.gist:
**Machine moulding** speeds up ramming and drawing: **jolt** (sand densest near the pattern), **squeeze** (densest at the top), **jolt-squeeze** (uniform) and **sand slinger** (large moulds).

**Special processes:**
- **CO₂ moulding**: sand with 3-6% **sodium silicate**, hardened in seconds by passing **CO₂** gas (a silica gel forms). Quick and strong; poor collapsibility.
- **Shell moulding (Croning)**: sand with 3-8% **phenolic resin** dropped on a metal pattern heated to about 200-250 °C forms a 5-10 mm shell; two shells are clamped together. Good finish and accuracy, mass production.
- **Investment (lost-wax)**: wax pattern, ceramic shell, wax melted out, shell fired, metal poured; intricate precise parts (turbine blades, jewellery).
- **Lost foam**: a polystyrene pattern vaporised by the metal. Permanent mould, die and centrifugal casting use metal moulds.

**Casting defects** (cause → remedy):
- **Blowholes**: moisture, low permeability, hard ramming, poor venting → control moisture, vent, ram correctly.
- **Shrinkage cavity**: poor feeding → proper risers, chills.
- **Misrun / cold shut**: metal too cold or poured too slowly → hotter, faster pour, better gating.
- **Hot tear**: restrained contraction → collapsible sand, fillets.
- **Mould shift / core shift**: misalignment → good dowels and pins, core prints, chaplets.
- **Swell**: soft ramming → ram uniformly.
- **Scab, rat tail, buckle**: sand expansion at the mould face → wood flour additive, less hard ramming.
- Also fins, sand and slag inclusions, metal penetration, fusion.

questions.q: Explain any five casting defects with their causes and remedies.
questions.a:
1. **Blowholes / gas porosity** (smooth rounded cavities, often near the top surface). Causes: excess moisture, low permeability, hard ramming, insufficient venting, damp cores. Remedies: control moisture, use permeable sand, ram correctly, vent adequately, dry cores.
2. **Shrinkage cavity** (rough, irregular voids at heavy sections). Causes: inadequate feeding during solidification. Remedies: correctly sized and placed risers, chills, directional solidification, uniform sections.
3. **Misrun / cold shut**. Causes: low pouring temperature, slow pouring, thin sections, poor fluidity, bad gating. Remedies: higher pouring temperature and rate, better gating, avoid very thin sections.
4. **Hot tear (pull crack)**. Causes: contraction restrained by hard mould or core while metal is weak, abrupt section changes. Remedies: collapsible sand (wood flour, sawdust), fillets, uniform sections, controlled cooling.
5. **Mould shift / mismatch**. Causes: cope and drag misaligned, worn dowels and box pins. Remedies: proper alignment pins, careful closing.
6. **Core shift**. Causes: wrong core prints, metal buoyancy. Remedies: proper core prints, chaplets.
7. **Swell**. Causes: soft ramming, metal pressure enlarges the cavity. Remedies: uniform, adequate ramming.
8. **Scab / rat tail / buckle**. Causes: expansion of silica sand at the mould face, hard ramming. Remedies: additives (wood flour, cereal), less hard ramming, proper sand.
9. **Inclusions (sand, slag)**. Causes: loose sand, erosion, slag entering. Remedies: strong mould, skimming, strainer cores, proper gating.
(Any five.)

questions.q: Describe the shell moulding process with its advantages.
questions.a:
**Process:**
1. A metal pattern (with gating) is heated to about 200-250 °C and sprayed with a silicone release agent.
2. It is clamped over a dump box containing fine dry silica sand mixed with 3-8% thermosetting phenolic resin.
3. The box is inverted; the sand falls on the hot pattern and a 5-10 mm layer partly cures in 15-30 s.
4. The box is turned back; excess sand falls away.
5. The shell on the pattern is cured in an oven (about 300 °C, a minute or two) and ejected.
6. Two matching shell halves are clamped or glued, backed with shot or sand, and poured.

**Advantages:** good surface finish and dimensional accuracy (±0.25 mm), thin sections possible, little machining, shells can be stored, high production rate, less sand used. **Limitations:** costly metal patterns and resin, limited casting size.

questions.q: Explain the CO₂ moulding process.
questions.a:
Clean dry silica sand is mixed with 3-6% sodium silicate (water glass) and rammed around the pattern as usual. CO₂ gas at about 1.5 bar is then passed through the mould (through vents or a probe) for 10-30 s. The gas reacts with the silicate:
$$\mathrm{Na_2SiO_3 + CO_2 \rightarrow Na_2CO_3 + SiO_2\ (gel)}$$
The silica gel binds the grains and hardens the mould within seconds, so no baking is needed. **Advantages:** quick, strong, accurate; good for cores and large moulds. **Limitations:** poor collapsibility (hard knock-out, risk of hot tears), sand not easily reclaimed, mould absorbs moisture if stored.
